title: Figure conventions and reproducibility
text: Documentation figures use R and ggplot2, with one shared theme in figures/style.R and explicit figure jobs in figures/render.R. Rust/PHP estimation has no graphics or R dependency. The .qmd walkthroughs still use Python for matrices and independent verification; a small bridge passes computed points to R for drawing. No ipynb files are maintained as documentation sources.

title: Figure conventions and reproducibility
text:
Visual conventions

Language comparisons keep R, Python, PHP in that order. Python is labeled statsmodels or SciPy reference to identify the actual implementation.
R uses blue circles (#0072B2); Python uses orange triangles (#D55E00); PHP uses green squares (#009E73). Color and shape reinforce the labels.
Conceptual figures use blue for the reference/population curve, green for the conditional/native curve, orange for an approximation or boundary, and gray for observations. Their legends describe the statistical quantity rather than imply that a curve is an implementation comparison.
Use a white background, common sans-serif type, restrained grids and explicit quantity/unit labels. Titles state what is shown; captions state the data or approximation, transformations and relevant limits.
Bar charts start at zero. Benchmark facets use their own labeled linear scales and show median bars plus actual timing repetitions. Missing memory is labeled unrecorded, not plotted as measured zero. A measured time of zero is marked 0* because timer resolution can hide a short fit.
Log scales are explicit and reserved for quantities spanning orders of magnitude, such as integration errors. The 1e-13 display floor in the quadrature-error plot is disclosed; it never changes stored numerical measurements.
Error-versus-reference figures use a zero reference line and label any unit multiplier. Agreement plots are not residual or model-adequacy diagnostics.

These conventions use ggplot2’s shared themes and explicit export controls. Each figure is saved as selectable-text SVG and a 160-dpi PNG, with fixed dimensions recorded in the figure manifest. Font family is generic sans-serif; the resolved font can differ across platforms.

title: Figure conventions and reproducibility
section: Generate figures without running fits or benchmarks
text:
Generate figures without running fits or benchmarks
Install the documentation-only R packages:
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "jsonlite", "svglite"),
                 repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
From the repository root:
Rscript docs/figures/render.R --all
# Or render an individual family/figure:
Rscript docs/figures/render.R ols
Rscript docs/figures/render.R approximation
Rscript docs/figures/render.R sleepstudy
./scripts/render-docs
The renderer reads saved benchmark/reference reports and notebook-exported points in figures/data/. It does not call estimators, regenerate reference fixtures or run timed workers. A changed numerical report requires refreshed plots; unchanged measurements should not be retimed for a style change.
The manifest records each input path/content MD5, image hashes, dimensions, renderer/theme hashes, R version, platform and direct package versions. The R package record also records installed transitive dependency versions. These are the versions used for the saved figures; installing another version is not a claim of byte-identical reproduction. Data/report provenance remains in its original statistical verification records.
Mathematical profile and posterior plots use points exported by the executable walkthroughs, preserving the visible calculations. Re-executing those .qmd pages updates their small JSON point snapshots and figures. Other figures read existing result reports. Jupyter embeds SVGs with namespaced clip IDs so figures on the same page do not interfere with each other.
Ordinary website rendering reuses frozen outputs and saved images. Neither R nor Python is required to browse the committed HTML. Re-executing computational notebooks still requires the documentation environment.

title: Figure conventions and reproducibility
text:
Existing figure coverage
The common renderer covers all five fixed/Gaussian-intercept benchmarks, the logistic-mixed benchmark, v0.1 preservation comparisons, Gaussian likelihood profiles, published-data numerical agreement, sleepstudy random slopes, logistic-mixed integration error, node sensitivity and conditional posterior shape. SVG and PNG downloads are retained alongside their saved input records.

title: Poisson regression verification record
text: The executed comparison fits identical observations in base R glm(), statsmodels GLM, and PHP fit_poisson(). The saved report records versions, complete outputs, maximum differences from R, warnings and retained-row metadata.

title: Poisson regression verification record
text:
Reference cases and conventions
Six saved R fixtures cover the simulated clinic sample, a single predictor, multiple predictors, no intercept, intercept only, correlated full-rank columns and sparse counts (the main sample is the multiple-predictor case). The three-way comparison adds listwise deletion of two rows. All coefficients, covariance entries, standard errors, normal z tests and p-values, Wald confidence limits, full fitted mean counts and response residuals, likelihood, deviance, null deviance, AIC and residual df are checked. Numerical tolerance is 1e-9 + 1e-7 × abs(reference); sample accounting is exact.
R uses confint.default(fit), not profile-likelihood confint(fit). Its fitting tolerance is 1e-16 to make covariance evaluated at the preceding IRLS iterate negligible. Iteration counts can differ across implementations; they are not a reference equality requirement. Without a ones column the null baseline is mean one; the Python runner computes this convention explicitly.

title: Poisson regression verification record
text:
Failure and integration checks
Rust/PHP tests reject insufficient observations, invalid shapes, nonfinite or negative/fractional outcomes, all-zero samples, dependent columns, and selected boundary designs. They check scaled predictor units, zero-count and near-fit deviance arithmetic, iteration exhaustion, missing-row warnings and alignment. OLS integration tests also run after changes to the shared PHP conversion code. No exhaustive finite-MLE existence test is supplied. Count overdispersion and sparse samples can invalidate conventional Wald inference. Offsets and exposure arguments are outside the first implementation. Linux and PHP-FPM deployment have not been exercised by these reports.

title: Poisson regression verification record
text:
Reproduce
From the repository root with matching PHP development tools:
export PHP=/opt/homebrew/bin/php
export PHP_CONFIG=/opt/homebrew/bin/php-config
cargo test --workspace --locked
cargo build -p phit --locked
php -n -d "extension=$PWD/target/debug/libphit.dylib" tests/poisson.php

QUARTO_PYTHON="$PWD/.context/notebooks-venv/bin/python" quarto render docs/notebooks/poisson-verification.qmd
Use .so on Linux. R fixture regeneration is an explicit development step: Rscript tests/generate-probit-poisson-fixtures.R. Ordinary Rust/PHP tests use saved fixtures without R or Python. See development for setup and large-sample benchmarks for additional evidence.

title: Binary logistic regression verification record
text:
Reference cases and conventions
Six saved R fixtures cover the simulated learning sample, a single predictor, multiple predictors, no intercept, intercept only, correlated full-rank columns and imbalanced outcomes (the main sample is the multiple-predictor case). The three-way comparison adds listwise deletion of two rows. All coefficients, covariance entries, standard errors, normal z tests and p-values, Wald confidence limits, full fitted probabilities and response residuals, likelihood, deviance, null deviance, AIC and residual df are checked. Numerical tolerance is 1e-9 + 1e-7 × abs(reference); sample accounting is exact.
R uses confint.default(fit), not profile-likelihood confint(fit). Its fitting tolerance is 1e-14 to make covariance evaluated at the preceding IRLS iterate negligible. Iteration counts can differ across implementations; they are not a reference equality requirement. Without a ones column the null baseline is probability 0.5; the Python runner computes this convention explicitly.

title: Binary logistic regression verification record
text:
Failure and integration checks
Rust/PHP tests reject insufficient observations, invalid shapes, nonfinite or nonbinary outcomes, one-class samples, dependent columns, and selected complete and quasi-separated designs. They check scaled predictor units, stable arithmetic at extreme logits, iteration exhaustion, missing-row warnings and alignment. OLS integration tests also run after changes to the shared PHP conversion code. No penalties or Firth correction are supplied. The separation check is not an exhaustive LP detector, and Wald inference can be poor with sparse or near-separated samples. Linux and PHP-FPM deployment have not been exercised by these reports.

title: Distribution and utility verification
text:
Reference generation and limitations
tests/generate-distribution-fixtures.R produces 553 distribution cases: R d/p/q functions at saved explicit parameter sets and evaluation points, including tiny probabilities, large counts/shapes, support boundaries and point masses. The same generator writes eight univariate, three paired and two weighted descriptive cases using seed 20261012. Numeric JSON inputs are parsed with serde_json float-roundtrip support so that Rust and PHP use the intended binary64 values.
docs/verifications/compare_distributions.py evaluates closed-form densities and regularized incomplete-beta/gamma tails using mpmath at 60 digits. Continuous reference quantiles use independently evaluated log-tail Newton iterations, starting from native/R/SciPy candidates but accepting only a high-precision tail residual. Discrete references verify the CDF-step inequality. Values are rounded once to binary64. A computation timeout or unavailable reference is recorded as null, never replaced by the native value. The 27 unavailable points remain visible in the report; their ordinary tests use the saved R reference and explicit identities. Subnormal values have fewer significant bits, so relative-error claims are limited.
The provenance manifest indexes all R/SciPy/mpmath and descriptive inputs, quantities, versions, generators, tolerance policies and hashes. The independent reference fixture SHA-256 values are also recorded in the native refresh report. --stored-references re-evaluates PHP without changing those values.
# Intentional independent reference regeneration (may take substantial time):
Rscript tests/generate-distribution-fixtures.R
PHP=/path/to/matching/php .context/v02/python/bin/python docs/verifications/compare_distributions.py
# Routine native refresh against existing references:
PHP=/path/to/matching/php .context/v02/python/bin/python docs/verifications/compare_distributions.py --stored-references
python3 scripts/reference-manifest.py
python3 scripts/distribution-docs.py
The optional Python environment needs NumPy, SciPy and mpmath; pins are in tests/benchmarks/distribution-requirements.txt. None are extension runtime or offline-test dependencies.

tests/distributions.php performs 8,618 comparisons under these original tolerances. When saved R and mpmath differ beyond tolerance, it uses the immutable mpmath value (25 independently adjudicated points). Forty-three documented boundary differences have separate conventions/identity checks. Scalar/batch values must be identical, including NAN/INF conventions where applicable. The suite also checks CDF/SF sums, quantile inverses and monotonicity, direct log functions, degenerate cases, argument names/defaults, array order and invalid input/error categories. An overflowing size-plus-mean NB conversion is checked to avoid a false point mass.
Rust independently checks extreme Student-t quantiles against mpmath, probability identities, validation and scaled-density underflow. The diagnostic R-comparison test reports raw worst errors including intended differences; it is not the sole correctness gate. PHP’s strict reference/identity suite is required as well.
tests/descriptive.php adds 145 R comparisons and missing/error checks. crates/stats-core/tests/descriptive.rs covers the same stored examples plus overflow and degenerate cases. The release gate includes both PHP suites, the Rust tests and the runnable distribution example. Descriptive conventions explain sample/population and frequency/reliability definitions.

title: Distribution and utility verification
text:
Documented reference differences

Discrete quantile p=1 for a point mass returns its mass location. R/SciPy may instead return the generic upper-support bound, including infinity.
R’s F density at +INF is NAN; the native API returns zero there.
R F quantiles can round to zero for tiny probabilities and small numerator df, where the native/mpmath value is a representable positive value.
R’s Student-t quantile at df=0.5 has a small nonzero center and selected far-tail inaccuracies. Native centering and high-precision tail checks establish the chosen values.
R’s discrete-quantile probability adjustment near 1 - 2^-52 can shift the returned count. Native uses a relative 64*EPSILON allowance on the smaller tail.
R’s mean-form negative-binomial mass approximation for size much larger than the observed count differs from the independent high-precision calculation.
SciPy’s large-df chi-square CDF has about 8.16e-9 relative error at the saved five-standard-deviation lower-tail point. The native and R results match mpmath much more closely. The benchmark records the same peer discrepancy without weakening native comparison tolerances.

Raw values and per-point errors remain in the fixtures/report. Intentional conventions and peer-library errors are distinct from unsupported reference points.

title: Distribution and utility verification
text:
Backend and model-path audit
The raw statrs report and executable crates/stats-core/examples/statrs_audit.rs document why statrs alone is not used for the new distribution API. The reuse experiment compares the public Normal log-CDF and Student-t quantile with the existing probit and OLS formulas. Candidate t quantiles improve large-df reference error, but all six tested critical values and 17 tested normal log-CDF values differ in rounding. The current release retains the established regression paths and their behavior. This is an evaluated compatibility decision, not an untested refactor.
cargo run -p stats-core --release --locked --example statrs_audit
cargo run -p stats-core --release --locked --example distribution_reuse_audit

title: v0.2 numerical API assessment (historical)
text:
Note



This record was written from 2026-10-12 to 2026-10-17, before the first tagged release. It describes the code and evidence as they were then, and is kept as history. The API overview and verification pages describe the current releases.
The distribution and statistical utility implementation includes probability evaluation, descriptive/draw kernels and explicitly seeded batch sampling. The native release gate passes on this Apple Silicon/macOS workstation with PHP 8.5.10 and matching headers: 68 Rust tests, 14 PHP suites and eleven executed examples passed, along with clippy, signatures, provenance and evidence-table checks. This is a source/readiness record; no tag, registry submission, binary publication or deployment was performed. Cargo/PIE version metadata still identifies the existing 0.1.0 baseline until the project’s separate release/versioning step.

title: v0.2 numerical API assessment (historical)
text:
Numerical findings and fixes
The saved native/mpmath errors are typically below 1e-13; the largest is about 8.34e-13 in a large-df chi-square log tail. Native tests keep the original operation-specific 1e-12 tolerances. R and SciPy have documented endpoint and tail differences, with an independent reference used only when the saved references justify it. In particular, SciPy’s large-df chi-square lower-tail error is visible in both the reference record and benchmarks. Unavailable high-precision values are recorded as null, and reduced subnormal precision is disclosed.
Additional verification fixed two arithmetic bugs: overflowing descriptive variance no longer becomes zero through max(NAN, 0), and finite large NB size/mean values whose sum overflows no longer become a false point mass. Negative descriptive weights are rejected before missing-value deletion. R reference values at ordinary scales remain within the established tolerances; existing regression APIs and numerical paths are preserved.

title: v0.2 numerical API assessment (historical)
text:
Reuse and RNG decisions
The executable reuse experiment found that the new Student-t quantile improves R agreement for the six tested OLS critical values, but changes their rounding. The public normal log-CDF differs at 17 saved points from the established probit calculation. This task also requires preserving regression behavior, so neither path is replaced in this release. A future refactor can use this evidence to make an explicit model compatibility decision.
Random sampling is implemented with dist_{family}_rng(n, seed, ...parameters). Each call owns a pinned ChaCha20 stream and transforms open-interval uniforms through the existing inverse CDF. The sampling contract defines seed ownership, count/type/range policies and reproducibility limits. Independent Python ChaCha/PCG/Open01 equations and base-R quantiles verify the stream and samples; benchmarks verify sampled points and full-vector moments before recording seeded-call timings. The earlier handoff recommendation to defer RNG has been superseded by this implementation.

text:
Release and platform limits
The new completion run verifies macOS arm64/PHP 8.5.10. Earlier packaging evidence in deployment covers Linux arm64 PHP 8.3/8.4/8.5 for the preceding source snapshot. That historical evidence does not establish that the latest hardening changes passed those environments. The configured remote amd64/PHP matrix and updated binary/container builds must run as part of the separate release process. Windows/ZTS remain outside the supported package matrix. Benchmarks do not establish performance bounds on other machines or all finite/extreme arguments.
Version/tag selection, Packagist registration and release/binary publication remain external release steps. No commit, push, PR or publication is part of this work.

title: Seeded batch sampling
text: Every supported distribution has a dist_{family}_rng() function that returns ordinary PHP numeric arrays. Sampling uses mature Rust RNG libraries already in the dependency graph: pinned rand 0.9.5 and rand_chacha 0.9.0, now explicit stats-core dependencies. No package versions were upgraded. Each call owns and restarts its own ChaCha20 state from the supplied seed.

title: Seeded batch sampling
text:
API and state ownership
The signature is dist_{family}_rng(int $n, int $seed, ...distribution parameters): array. The family parameters and defaults are exactly those of the corresponding probability API.
$normal = Phit\dist_normal_rng(n: 5, seed: 42); // Default mean 0, SD 1.
$measurements = Phit\dist_normal_rng(n: 8, seed: 20261012, mean: 10, sd: .5);
$counts = Phit\dist_poisson_rng(n: 8, seed: 20261013, lambda: 3.2);
$beta = Phit\dist_beta_rng(n: 8, seed: 17, alpha: 2, beta: 5);

mean = 0, sd = 1

n is an integer in [0,1000000]; seed is a nonnegative PHP integer, including zero, up to PHP_INT_MAX (2^63−1 on the supported 64-bit platforms). Both arguments are required. Every successful result is a packed list<float> of exactly n finite values; discrete counts are also floats. There is no scalar sampling form or additional _array suffix because sampling is already a batch operation.
The same seed and parameters reproduce exactly the same result within the same build. Asking for fewer samples returns the prefix of a longer call. Calls for other families or seeds do not advance a shared stream. PHP’s mt_srand() and application RNG state are not read or changed.
Because a seed selects the same underlying uniform sequence across families, reusing it deliberately couples results through their quantiles. Use distinct seeds for separate batches when independent streams are intended. There is no implicit time-based seed, OS entropy lookup, retained RNG object or hidden global state. The runnable examples/rng.php verifies repeatability and prefix behavior.

title: Seeded batch sampling
text:
Uniform, categorical and permutation sampling
Four samplers have no probability API. They take the same n and seed arguments, have the same limits, and consume one uniform from the same stream per draw.








Function
R equivalent
Returns




dist_uniform_rng(n, seed, min = 0, max = 1)
runif(n, min, max)
list<float>


dist_categorical_rng(n, seed, prob)
sample(length(prob), n, replace = TRUE, prob = prob) - 1
list<int>


dist_categorical_rows_rng(seed, prob)
one sample(K, 1, prob = prob[i, ]) - 1 per row

$x = Phit\dist_uniform_rng(n: 5, seed: 1, min: -1, max: 1);
$categories = ['returns', 'sizing', 'quality'];
$picked = array_map(fn ($k) => $categories[$k],
    Phit\dist_categorical_rng(n: 5, seed: 2, prob: [.2, .5, .3]));
// One rating per review, each from its own probabilities.
$ratings = Phit\dist_categorical_rows_rng(seed: 3, prob: [[.1, .6, .3], [.7, .2, .1]]);
$shuffled = Phit\permutation_rng(n: 10, seed: 4); // All of 0..9.
$subset = Phit\permutation_rng(n: 10, seed: 4, size: 3); // Its first three.
Indices are 0-based positions, so they index PHP lists directly. Add one for R’s 1-based categories.

Uniform. Each draw is min + (max - min) * u, as in R’s runif(). min must not exceed max, and min == max gives min.
Categorical. prob is a list of finite, nonnegative weights with a positive sum. As in R’s sample(), the weights are divided by their sum. The draw for u is the first index k with u * sum(prob) < prob[0] + ... + prob[k]. A zero weight is never drawn. If rounding puts u * sum(prob) at or above the sum, the last positive weight is drawn.
Rows. dist_categorical_rows_rng() takes a list of up to one million such vectors and returns one draw per row. Rows may have different lengths. Draw i uses the ith uniform, so a list of equal rows gives dist_categorical_rng()’s result for the same seed.
Permutation. permutation_rng() runs a partial Fisher–Yates shuffle of 0..n-1. Step i swaps position i with i + floor(u * (n - i)), capped at n - 1. size is in [0, n] and defaults to n. A smaller size returns the prefix of the full permutation.

These samplers use the same ChaCha20 uniforms as the other families. Their results therefore differ from R’s for the same seed, as the other families’ results do. A non-list prob, a negative weight, a zero sum, min > max, or size > n raises 1001. A nonfinite weight, weight sum, bound, or uniform draw raises 1003. More than one million draws or rows, or n above one million for a permutation, raises 1007.

title: Seeded batch sampling
text:
Numerical method and reproducibility
For every output, ChaCha20 provides a 64-bit word; rand’s Open01<f64> maps its upper 52 bits to a midpoint strictly inside (0,1). The value is transformed by the existing validated inverse CDF. The algorithm consumes one uniform per sample, including point masses. This uses the established numerical quantile kernels for all 13 parameterizations, without introducing a separate distribution backend.
The open interval excludes infinite support endpoints. The finite uniform grid also limits represented tail probabilities: its minimum is 2^-53 and its maximum is 1−2^-53. This implementation favors a small, consistent numerical path over distribution-specific rejection samplers; benchmarks record the cost for normal, beta and Poisson batches.
The pinned rand_core seed_from_u64 expands the integer with its documented PCG32 mapping into the 256-bit ChaCha key. Exact uniform vectors are checked independently in Python. Dependency or quantile-algorithm changes can change seeded samples and must be reviewed as reproducibility changes. Bitwise transformed-sample agreement across different library versions, compilers or platform math libraries is not promised; seeds are not claimed to match R or NumPy’s unrelated default engines. The full dependency lock and algorithm are recorded for reproducible runs.

title: Seeded batch sampling
text:
Validation
Distribution parameter domains match probability evaluation. They are validated even when n is zero; valid empty requests return []. Negative n/seed raises 1001, a request above one million raises 1007, and nonfinite distribution parameters raise 1003. Scalar argument conversion/type failures follow the repository’s runtime-error convention (code zero) rather than StatsError categories.
A quantile that exceeds binary64 range raises 1003 and rejects the entire batch; no partial results, dropped samples or replacement infinities are returned. Very heavy tails/extreme scales can therefore fail even with finite parameters. Count precision follows the existing discrete-quantile convention and binary64 limits. The sampling limit bounds a single output allocation; callers retain control of overall workload and parameter coordinates.

title: Seeded batch sampling
text:
Independent verification
tests/generate-rng-fixtures.py independently implements the ChaCha20 block equations, PCG seed expansion and Open01 mapping. It never calls the extension or rand. tests/generate-rng-fixtures.R maps those saved uniforms through base-R quantiles. Python preserves full integer seeds and exact uniform bits while R supplies the independent transformed reference values.
The saved tests/fixtures/rng-python-r.json contains 25 cases, 2,000 values: 384 exact uniform values at four seeds (including zero and PHP_INT_MAX), all 13 families, three additional normal seed cases, and five point masses. Rust checks all values; PHP checks the 1,616 transformed references. Uniform/discrete values match exactly; continuous reference tolerance is 1e-15 + 1e-12*abs(reference). Both suites check repeatability, prefixes, state isolation, domains/limits and nonfinite samples. The uniform, categorical and permutation samplers are checked against the documented maps applied to the fixture’s Python uniforms. Deterministic normal/Poisson moment checks complement the reference vectors. PHP additionally verifies parameter names/defaults and strict seed/count types.

title: Distributions, statistics, draws, optimization and CSV
text:
Thirteen distribution parameterizations expose seven operations, each in scalar and _array form: 182 functions in total. Continuous families use pdf, logpdf, cdf, logcdf, sf, logsf, quantile; discrete families replace pdf/logpdf with pmf/logpmf. Names follow dist_{family}_{operation} and dist_{family}_{operation}_array. The distribution contract lists every family, parameter name/default, domain and support. The generated stubs/phit.php is the exact signature reference.
Numeric arguments/elements accept PHP integers or floats; binomial size is an integer in [0,2^53]. Batch results are packed lists preserving iteration order, with keys discarded. Empty input returns an empty result after parameter validation. Null, NAN and malformed elements reject the entire batch; there is no row deletion or missing policy. Distribution evaluation points may be ±INF; parameters must be finite. Invalid domains raise 1001, NAN points/nonfinite parameters raise 1003, unsupported binomial size raises 1007, and a NAN numerical result raises 1006. Boundary densities/log values can legitimately be ±INF. Discrete quantiles are floats with a 64*EPSILON relative allowance at CDF steps. Degenerate distributions return their point mass at quantile p=1, even where R/SciPy differ.
The ten descriptive functions are mean, variance, SD, covariance, correlation, scalar/batch type-7 quantiles, median, weighted mean and weighted variance. They default to missing: 'raise', with explicit 'drop' deletion, pairwise for aligned inputs. Variance/SD/covariance defaults to sample normalization; weighted variance defaults to frequency weighting, with reliability and population options. Missing null/NAN raises 1001 by default; infinity always raises 1003. Constant-input correlation is explicitly NAN. Other nonfinite arithmetic raises 1003, rather than allowing overflow to appear as zero variance. Negative weights are rejected before missing-value deletion. These policies differ from regression defaults and from strict literal draw kernels, and are not inferred from input shape.
Each family also exposes dist_{family}_rng(int $n, int $seed, ...parameters): array, with the same distribution parameters/defaults. n is in [0,1000000], seed is a nonnegative PHP integer, and every call owns local ChaCha20 state. Successful results are packed lists of n finite floats, including discrete counts. Repeated seed/parameters reproduce prefixes within the pinned build; empty batches still validate parameters. Negative count/seed raises 1001, excessive count raises 1007, and nonfinite parameters/generated samples raise 1003. Runtime argument-conversion errors retain code zero. The sampling contract defines the inverse-CDF method, finite uniform grid and version/platform reproducibility limits.
All calls are stateless with respect to the caller’s PHP RNG state. The reference record, benchmarks and v0.2 assessment distinguish implemented behavior, verified accuracy and publication/platform limits.

title: R compatibility: target, coverage and remaining work
text:
The target is equivalent statistical results for equivalent supplied numerical designs in R and this extension. Full R/lme4 compatibility is a project goal, not a claim about the current release. This expansion adds tested functionality; the open items below remain part of the goal. Base R’s stats package supplies lm() and glm(); lme4 is an additional R package.
The native API remains ordinary arrays. Formulas, factor encoding and R’s S3/S4 model objects are separate concerns; matching estimation does not require making PHP impersonate R. A helper can construct designs, proportions/trial counts and nested grouping identifiers without changing the estimator. See the contracts and design philosophy.

title: R compatibility: target, coverage and remaining work
text:
Distribution and statistical utility compatibility
The v0.2 probability APIs cover the planned distribution families with scalar/batch density, mass, tail and quantile operations. Descriptive statistics follow sample variance/covariance and R type-7 quantiles, with explicit frequency/reliability/population weight definitions. R and independent 60-digit mpmath fixtures verify ordinary and extreme values; the comparison record documents intentional point-mass/endpoint differences, R inaccuracies and SciPy peer discrepancies. This numerical coverage does not implement R recycling, coercion, vector names or formulas. Seeded sampling uses local ChaCha20 state; its sequences are independent of R’s RNG algorithms/state. Existing model paths and their behavior remain unchanged; the estimator reuse experiment is recorded in the v0.2 assessment.

The new mixed call is fit_mixed(). The existing fit_mixed_intercept() remains the optimized one-group random-intercept ML call used by the million-row benchmarks. The general implementation caches a dense QR square-root summary and then solves penalized least squares; it does not allocate an observation covariance matrix. It has explicit dense-design limits: at most 512 random coefficients and 50,000,000 entries in the initial augmented matrix. This is not yet lme4’s sparse implementation and has not been benchmarked on large general designs.
An intercept-only OLS fit now reports R-squared and adjusted R-squared as zero, matching summary.lm(). Other undefined statistics retain their documented NAN/INF representation. This is a documented change to the previous intercept-only zero-response R-squared convention.

title: R compatibility: target, coverage and remaining work
text:
Evidence and tolerance policy
The executed comparison notebook fits 12 fixed-model cases and 15 mixed-model cases, including the published sleepstudy random-slope model under both ML and REML, plus three- and four-grouping-level nested designs. It checks coefficients, covariance, inference, every observation’s fitted/residual values, random effects/covariances, scale, likelihood and information criteria. Both native optimizers are compared against all four R wrappers. sleepstudy ML/REML also have independent statsmodels fits. Older fixtures and the four published random-intercept datasets remain tested.
Fixed-model comparisons use abs_error <= 1e-7 + 1e-6 * abs(reference). Native BOBYQA versus R BOBYQA uses 1e-5 + 1e-5 * abs(reference) for mixed estimates; cross-optimizer comparisons use 1e-3 + 3e-4 * abs(reference). All mixed likelihood/AIC/BIC comparisons use the stricter 5e-6 + 1e-9 * abs(reference). Shapes, sample metadata, grouping order, parameter counts and singular flags are exact where compared. The notebook reports actual errors, not only pass/fail.
GLM covariances are evaluated at the final coefficients. R’s vcov() for a glm reuses the weights of the last IRLS iteration, which were computed one step before the final update. On well-conditioned fits the two agree far inside the tolerance. On designs near separation they can differ by about 1e-5 relative. For am ~ factor(cyl) + wt on mtcars, the Fisher information recomputed in R at coef(fit) matches the phit covariance to about 1e-9.
Different optimizers can stop at slightly different variance estimates on a flat likelihood. The cross-optimizer tolerance accommodates that observed spread, particularly covariance entries and small residuals on sleepstudy. It does not replace the stricter BOBYQA check or likelihood check.
The R fixtures record each wrapper’s controls and warnings. They use tightened optimization controls and boundary.tol=1e-3, with lme4 checking whether snapping near-boundary Cholesky parameters to zero improves the objective. At the default boundary tolerance, one singular REML case was left just above zero by nloptwrap and classified nonsingular. Tightening nlminb excessively also produced singular convergence warnings. These fixtures validate explicit controls, not identity under every package default. The saved reference runs have convergence code zero and no warnings. The multi-level BOBYQA references also use a local R-only restart (rhobeg=0.001, rhoend=1e-9) to improve variance-component precision on flat profiles; no native estimates are used to seed R. Published historical benchmark reports retain their original model/optimizer definitions; their timings do not describe the new general fitter.

title: R compatibility: target, coverage and remaining work
text:
Remaining compatibility work
The following items are not implemented and are not covered by a blanket parity claim:

Native NLopt and PORT/nlminb backends, full optimizer controls, restart policies, gradient/Hessian convergence diagnostics, and an allFit-style runtime audit.
Sparse general mixed-model computation and large-design verification.
R-style handling of zero weights, aliased/rank-deficient fixed columns, zero-column designs, and fit objects retained after nonconvergence. We currently reject these or fail with an explicit error rather than returning unreliable inference.
Configurable confidence levels; profile and bootstrap intervals; likelihood-ratio comparisons and fixed-effect degrees-of-freedom corrections. Mixed Wald p-values are an explicit extension; lme4’s default Gaussian summary does not supply them.
Simulation on new observations, prediction standard errors and intervals for mixed models, residual diagnostics, leverage/influence, and model-object methods such as update/refit/anova. (predict() covers point predictions, standard errors and lm intervals for new data, as described with the formulas; random-effect conditional variances are reported by the mixed fits.)
Formula parsing, contrasts and factor encoding, subset/na.exclude semantics, multivariate lm responses, fractional binomial weights and additional GLM families/links.
Broader generalized/nonlinear mixed models: binomial random slopes/multiple terms, mixed Poisson/probit/negative-binomial likelihoods, nlmer, and related methods. The new binomial random-intercept glmer counterpart is implemented separately, with Laplace/adaptive quadrature; it does not yet support the general Gaussian random-term designs.

Each addition needs an input/output contract, a mathematical walkthrough, saved R reference cases and PHP integration checks. This document is the compatibility ledger: move an item to implemented only when that evidence exists.

Each estimator is fitted with an intercept and without one. Binary estimators include both individual binary responses and grouped success proportions. Weights and offsets affect the fit, covariance, null model and likelihood. We check those quantities rather than testing only unweighted coefficients.
For grouped binomial rows with s successes out of m trials, supply y=s/m and weight=m. R’s equivalent calls are:
#| eval: false
fit <- glm(proportion ~ study + practice,
           family=binomial("logit"), weights=trials, offset=known_offset,
           data=observations, control=glm.control(epsilon=1e-12, maxit=200))
# binomial("probit") selects the normal-CDF link instead.
coef(fit)
vcov(fit)
logLik(fit)
fit$deviance
fit$null.deviance
A Poisson exposure e contributes log(e) to the linear predictor; a prior weight instead multiplies that observation’s likelihood. Those are different operations. For weighted OLS, residual variance is sigma²/w_i and likelihood includes the weight determinant. Full generator code is in tests/generate-r-compatibility-fixtures.R.

    x: $fixedDesign,
    y: $scores,
    random: [
        ['z' => $ones, 'groups' => $districtIds],
        ['z' => $ones, 'groups' => $districtSchoolKeys],
        ['z' => $ones, 'groups' => $districtSchoolClassKeys],
        ['z' => $ones, 'groups' => $districtSchoolClassStudentKeys],
    ],
    reml: true,
);
The equivalent R random-intercept specification is (1 | district/school/class/student). Nesting does not introduce a correlation parameter between the levels; each term has its own variance. Random slopes can also be supplied through each term’s z columns, subject to identifiability and size limits. The current dense implementation supports at most 512 total random coefficients and 50,000,000 initial augmented matrix entries.

title: Probit: a normal latent variable and Fisher scoring
text:
We observe simulated students, with study hours, a practice score and a binary pass/fail outcome. Inputs are observed data, not guesses. The column of ones is constructed to estimate an intercept. R seed 20261013 generates 120 students: hours are uniform between 1 and 12, scores are clipped to 20–95 from 45 + 3 × hours + normal noise with standard deviation 8. Both are rounded to two decimals.
The underlying simulation is a latent normal threshold model:
\[z_i^*=-1.9+0.13\,\mathrm{hours}_i+0.011\,\mathrm{score}_i+\epsilon_i,
\quad \epsilon_i\sim N(0,1),\quad y_i=\mathbf{1}\{z_i^*>0\}.\]
With \(\eta_i=x_i^\top\beta\), symmetry of the standard normal gives \(P(y_i=1)=P(\epsilon_i>-\eta_i)=\Phi(\eta_i)\). The latent value is a model construction: only the resulting 0 or 1 is supplied to the estimator. Fixing the latent variance to one identifies the coefficient scale; there is no sigma to estimate.
The normal CDF \(\Phi(a)\) is the area under a standard-normal density to the left of \(a\). The density is \(\phi(a)=e^{-a^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\), and \(\Phi'(a)=\phi(a)\). Unlike a logit coefficient, \(e^{\beta_j}\) is not a constant odds multiplier. The local probability slope is \(\phi(\eta_i)\beta_j\), so it varies by observation.

title: Probit: a normal latent variable and Fisher scoring
text:
2. Likelihood and derivatives
For independent Bernoulli outcomes the log-likelihood is
\[\ell(\beta)=\sum_i[y_i\log\Phi(\eta_i)+(1-y_i)\log\Phi(-\eta_i)].\]
The complement is written \(\Phi(-\eta)\) to avoid subtracting a CDF rounded to one. Taking a derivative with respect to \(\eta_i\) gives
\[s_i=\phi(\eta_i)\frac{y_i-\pi_i}{\pi_i(1-\pi_i)},\qquad
\pi_i=\Phi(\eta_i),\qquad g=X^\top s.\]
For a success this is \(\phi/\Phi(\eta)\); for a failure it is \(-\phi/\Phi(-\eta)\). These ratios are evaluated from log density minus log tail probability. Rust uses erfc for ordinary tails and a normal Mills-ratio continued fraction beyond -8, preserving finite log-likelihoods even when the CDF underflows.
Expected negative curvature, or Fisher information, is
\[I=X^\top W X,\qquad
w_i=\frac{\phi(\eta_i)^2}{\pi_i(1-\pi_i)}.\]
One way to see this is to square \(s_i\) and take its expectation: \(E[(y_i-\pi_i)^2]=\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\), leaving the expression above. Unlike canonical logistic regression, observed curvature and expected information need not agree at a finite probit sample. We use Fisher scoring and its covariance, matching R glm and statsmodels GLM; a discrete-model probit fit’s observed-Hessian covariance can differ without either calculation being erroneous.

title: Probit: a normal latent variable and Fisher scoring
text:
3. Scoring, weighted matrices and SVD
Fisher scoring solves \(I\Delta\beta=g\) and updates coefficients. For Poisson this is also the Newton step, since information equals negative Hessian. To avoid forming and inverting the cross-product for fitting, define column scales \(D\), \(A=XD^{-1}\) and \(\theta=D\beta\). Solve
\[B\Delta\theta\approx q,\quad B=W^{1/2}A,\quad q=W^{-1/2}s,
\qquad B=USV^\top,\quad \Delta\theta=VS^{-1}U^\top q.\]
The weighted least-squares normal equations are \(A^\top W A\Delta\theta=A^\top s\). This is the same update in scaled coordinates, with \(\Delta\beta=D^{-1}\Delta\theta\). We display cross-products to understand them; the production solve uses weighted SVD. See the OLS SVD explanation.
Weights and scores change each iteration: this is IRLS. The full increment can overshoot, so a decreasing-likelihood step is halved, at most 30 times. Both a small full coefficient increment and a small likelihood change are required. A tiny damped step alone does not establish convergence; the limit is 100 updates.

def values(eta):
    log_density = -0.5*eta**2-0.5*np.log(2*np.pi)
    probability = ndtr(eta)
    root = np.exp(log_density-0.5*(log_ndtr(eta)+log_ndtr(-eta)))
    score = np.where(y == 1, np.exp(log_density-log_ndtr(eta)), -np.exp(log_density-log_ndtr(-eta)))
    return probability,root,score

def log_likelihood(eta):
    return np.where(y == 1,log_ndtr(eta),log_ndtr(-eta)).sum()

scales = np.linalg.norm(X,axis=0)
A = X/scales
theta = np.zeros(p)
history=[]
for iteration in range(1,101):
    eta=A@theta
    fitted,root,score=values(eta)
    B=root[:,None]*A
    q=score/root
    U,singular,Vt=np.linalg.svd(B,full_matrices=False)
    assert np.all(singular > np.finfo(float).eps*max(n,p)*singular[0])
    step=Vt.T@((U.T@q)/singular)
    old_ll=log_likelihood(eta)
    fraction=1.0
    for _ in range(31):
        candidate=theta+fraction*step
        new_ll=log_likelihood(A@candidate)
        if np.isfinite(new_ll) and new_ll >= old_ll-16*np.finfo(float).eps*(1+abs(old_ll)): break
        fraction/=2
    else: raise RuntimeError("No improving step")
    if iteration==1:
        show_matrix(r"\beta^{(0)}",theta/scales)
        show_matrix(r"s^{(0)}",score)
        show_matrix(r"W^{(0)}_{1:5,1:5}\text{ (top-left block)}",np.diag(root[:5]**2))
        show_matrix(r"g^{(0)}=X^\top s",X.T@score)
        show_matrix(r"I^{(0)}=X^\top W X",X.T@(root[:,None]**2*X))
        for j in range(p): show_dot(rf"g_{{{j+1}}}",X[:,j],score)
        show_dot(r"I_{2,3}",X[:,1],root**2*X[:,2])
        show_matrix("B",B)
        show_matrix("q",q)
        show_matrix(r"U^\top q",U.T@q)
        show_matrix(r"\Delta\beta",step/scales)
    history.append({"iteration":iteration,"fraction":fraction,"log-likelihood":new_ll,
                    "intercept":candidate[0]/scales[0],"predictor 1":candidate[1]/scales[1],"predictor 2":candidate[2]/scales[2]})
    small=np.all(np.abs(step)<=1e-11*(1+np.abs(candidate)))
    small_ll=abs(new_ll-old_ll)<=1e-13*(1+abs(old_ll))
    theta=candidate
    if small and small_ll: break
else: raise RuntimeError("Did not converge")
beta=theta/scales
eta=X@beta
fitted,root,score=values(eta)
display(pd.DataFrame(history))
show_matrix(r"\hat\beta",beta)
show_matrix(r"X^\top s\text{ at final fit}",X.T@score)
show_dot(r"\hat\eta_1",X[0],beta)
print("First fitted probability:",fitted[0])

title: Probit: a normal latent variable and Fisher scoring
text:
4. Covariance and Wald inference
Evaluate information at the final coefficients, then compute
\[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)=I(\hat\beta)^{-1},\quad
\operatorname{SE}_j=\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)_{jj}},\quad
z_j=\hat\beta_j/\operatorname{SE}_j.\]
The SVD supplies the covariance as \(D^{-1}VS^{-2}V^\top D^{-1}\). Two-sided p-values use \(2P(Z\ge |z_j|)\) and 95% Wald limits use \(\hat\beta_j\pm1.959964\operatorname{SE}_j\). These are asymptotic normal tests, not OLS Student t tests. We do not multiply covariance by RSS/(n-p). R confint.default() supplies equivalent Wald intervals; ordinary GLM confint() uses profile likelihood instead.

title: Probit: a normal latent variable and Fisher scoring
text:
5. Likelihood, deviance and AIC
For individual binary outcomes the saturated likelihood is zero, giving \(D=-2\ell(\hat\beta)\). The intercept-only null probability is the observed success proportion. Without a ones column, the null baseline is 0.5. Neither a latent variance nor an OLS residual variance is estimated. A probit coefficient is on the latent normal scale: multiplying it by a normal density converts it to a local probability slope, not an odds ratio.
AIC is \(2p-2\ell(\hat\beta)\); residual degrees of freedom are \(n-p\), without an estimated dispersion parameter. Predictions are probabilities, and residuals are observed minus fitted. These vectors follow retained input row order.

                deviance=model_deviance,null_deviance=null_deviance,aic=2*p-2*ll,df_residual=n-p)
for key,value in calculated.items():
    np.testing.assert_allclose(value,case["expected"][key],atol=1e-9,rtol=1e-7,err_msg=key)

title: Probit: a normal latent variable and Fisher scoring
text:
6. Assumptions, failure modes and experiments
Both observed classes must remain after missing-row deletion. Complete or quasi separation can make a finite MLE nonexistent; encountered separating directions are rejected, as are singular information and iteration exhaustion. This certificate check is not exhaustive separation detection. Near separation can produce poor Wald inference even for a converged fit. Try replacing passed by study_hours > 6: what would happen to the latent coefficient as the probabilities approach the labels?
For both methods the retained design must have n > p and full numerical rank. Missing null/NAN rows are dropped with a warning unless missing: ‘raise’. No partial unconverged result is returned. See the contract and the executed three-way comparison.

title: Probit: a normal latent variable and Fisher scoring
text:
Rust connections
fit_probit owns its input vectors and converts them to nalgebra matrices. Borrowed matrix operands remain available for later iterations; iterators construct weights and score residuals. A dedicated loop performs this estimator’s updates. Result and ? propagate validation/numerical failures. The returned struct holds numeric fields; the PHP binding converts those fields into an associative array and adds warning/sample metadata. No generic optimizer or family hierarchy is added. See Rust learning notes and crates/stats-core/src/probit.rs.
Reference documentation: R glm, R families, statsmodels GLM.

title: Poisson: count likelihood, log link and IRLS
text:
We observe simulated clinic days, with daily visitors, a staffing measure and the number of calls received. These are synthetic counts, not patient records. R seed 20261014 generates 120 days. Visitors are rounded uniform draws between 80 and 300; staffing is visitors/50 plus normal noise with standard deviation 0.8, clipped to 2–10 and rounded to two decimals. Counts are independent draws from
\[y_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_i),\qquad
\log\mu_i=0.1+0.005\,\mathrm{visitors}_i-0.12\,\mathrm{staff}_i.\]
Inputs and outcomes are data. The supplied ones column estimates the intercept. Known generating parameters are distinct from fitted estimates, which vary by sample. The outcome is a nonnegative integer; the fitted mean \(\mu_i\) is a positive real number, not a rounded count or a probability. Under the model, \(E[y_i\mid x_i]=\operatorname{Var}(y_i\mid x_i)=\mu_i\).
The log link is \(\eta_i=x_i^\top\beta=\log\mu_i\), so \(\mu_i=e^{\eta_i}\). Holding other predictors fixed, a one-unit increase multiplies the mean by \(e^{\beta_j}\). A negative staffing coefficient here describes a conditional association, not a causal staffing effect. This first API has no exposure/offset argument: a constant exposure is implicit, and these are daily counts, not rates.

title: Poisson: count likelihood, log link and IRLS
text:
2. Likelihood and derivatives
The probability of one count is
\[P(y_i\mid\mu_i)=\frac{e^{-\mu_i}\mu_i^{y_i}}{y_i!}.\]
Taking logs and substituting \(\mu_i=e^{\eta_i}\) gives
\[\ell(\beta)=\sum_i[y_i\eta_i-e^{\eta_i}-\log\Gamma(y_i+1)].\]
For integer counts \(\Gamma(y_i+1)=y_i!\). The factorial term does not change the coefficient optimum, but must remain in reported likelihood and AIC. Rust uses statrs::function::gamma::ln_gamma instead of forming a huge factorial.
Since \(d e^{\eta_i}/d\eta_i=e^{\eta_i}=\mu_i\), the first derivative is \(y_i-\mu_i\). Applying \(d\eta_i/d\beta_j=x_{ij}\) gives
\[g=X^\top(y-\mu),\qquad H=-X^\top W X,\qquad
W=\operatorname{diag}(\mu_i).\]
Observed and expected information coincide here: \(I=-H=X^\top W X\). There is no OLS estimate of error variance; Poisson dispersion is fixed at one. Actual count data with overdispersion can have understated conventional standard errors. Robust covariance and negative-binomial models are outside this implementation.

title: Poisson: count likelihood, log link and IRLS
text:
3. Scoring, weighted matrices and SVD
Fisher scoring solves \(I\Delta\beta=g\) and updates coefficients. For Poisson this is also the Newton step, since information equals negative Hessian. To avoid forming and inverting the cross-product for fitting, define column scales \(D\), \(A=XD^{-1}\) and \(\theta=D\beta\). Solve
\[B\Delta\theta\approx q,\quad B=W^{1/2}A,\quad q=W^{-1/2}s,
\qquad B=USV^\top,\quad \Delta\theta=VS^{-1}U^\top q.\]
The weighted least-squares normal equations are \(A^\top W A\Delta\theta=A^\top s\). This is the same update in scaled coordinates, with \(\Delta\beta=D^{-1}\Delta\theta\). We display cross-products to understand them; the production solve uses weighted SVD. See the OLS SVD explanation.
Weights and scores change each iteration: this is IRLS. The full increment can overshoot, so a decreasing-likelihood step is halved, at most 30 times. Both a small full coefficient increment and a small likelihood change are required. A tiny damped step alone does not establish convergence; the limit is 100 updates.

def values(eta):
    mean = np.exp(eta)
    return mean,np.exp(0.5*eta),y-mean

def log_likelihood(eta):
    return np.sum(y*eta-np.exp(eta)-gammaln(y+1))

scales = np.linalg.norm(X,axis=0)
A = X/scales
theta = np.zeros(p)
history=[]
for iteration in range(1,101):
    eta=A@theta
    fitted,root,score=values(eta)
    B=root[:,None]*A
    q=score/root
    U,singular,Vt=np.linalg.svd(B,full_matrices=False)
    assert np.all(singular > np.finfo(float).eps*max(n,p)*singular[0])
    step=Vt.T@((U.T@q)/singular)
    old_ll=log_likelihood(eta)
    fraction=1.0
    for _ in range(31):
        candidate=theta+fraction*step
        new_ll=log_likelihood(A@candidate)
        if np.isfinite(new_ll) and new_ll >= old_ll-16*np.finfo(float).eps*(1+abs(old_ll)): break
        fraction/=2
    else: raise RuntimeError("No improving step")
    if iteration==1:
        show_matrix(r"\beta^{(0)}",theta/scales)
        show_matrix(r"s^{(0)}",score)
        show_matrix(r"W^{(0)}_{1:5,1:5}\text{ (top-left block)}",np.diag(root[:5]**2))
        show_matrix(r"g^{(0)}=X^\top s",X.T@score)
        show_matrix(r"I^{(0)}=X^\top W X",X.T@(root[:,None]**2*X))
        for j in range(p): show_dot(rf"g_{{{j+1}}}",X[:,j],score)
        show_dot(r"I_{2,3}",X[:,1],root**2*X[:,2])
        show_matrix("B",B)
        show_matrix("q",q)
        show_matrix(r"U^\top q",U.T@q)
        show_matrix(r"\Delta\beta",step/scales)
    history.append({"iteration":iteration,"fraction":fraction,"log-likelihood":new_ll,
                    "intercept":candidate[0]/scales[0],"predictor 1":candidate[1]/scales[1],"predictor 2":candidate[2]/scales[2]})
    small=np.all(np.abs(step)<=1e-8*(1+np.abs(candidate)))
    small_ll=abs(new_ll-old_ll)<=1e-10*(1+abs(old_ll))
    theta=candidate
    if small and small_ll: break
else: raise RuntimeError("Did not converge")
beta=theta/scales
eta=X@beta
fitted,root,score=values(eta)

title: Poisson: count likelihood, log link and IRLS
text:
4. Covariance and Wald inference
Evaluate information at the final coefficients, then compute
\[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)=I(\hat\beta)^{-1},\quad
\operatorname{SE}_j=\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)_{jj}},\quad
z_j=\hat\beta_j/\operatorname{SE}_j.\]
The SVD supplies the covariance as \(D^{-1}VS^{-2}V^\top D^{-1}\). Two-sided p-values use \(2P(Z\ge |z_j|)\) and 95% Wald limits use \(\hat\beta_j\pm1.959964\operatorname{SE}_j\). These are asymptotic normal tests, not OLS Student t tests. We do not multiply covariance by RSS/(n-p). R confint.default() supplies equivalent Wald intervals; ordinary GLM confint() uses profile likelihood instead.

p_values=2*norm.sf(np.abs(z))
conf_int=np.column_stack([beta-norm.ppf(.975)*se,beta+norm.ppf(.975)*se])

show_matrix(r"\hat\mu\text{ or }\hat\pi",fitted)

title: Poisson: count likelihood, log link and IRLS
text:
5. Likelihood, deviance and AIC
The saturated model sets \(\mu_i=y_i\). Its log-likelihood is generally not zero:
\[\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}=\sum_i[y_i\log y_i-y_i-\log\Gamma(y_i+1)],\qquad
D=2(\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell(\hat\beta))
=2\sum_i[y_i\log(y_i/\hat\mu_i)-(y_i-\hat\mu_i)].\]
For zero counts use \(0\log0=0\), so the deviance contribution is \(2\hat\mu_i\). For \(y_i>0\), Rust writes \(d_i=\eta_i-\log y_i\) and evaluates the contribution as \(2y_i[\operatorname{expm1}(d_i)-d_i]\) to preserve precision near a fitted count. Unlike binary regression, Poisson deviance is not -2 × log-likelihood. An explicit intercept gives null mean \(\bar y\); without it the null mean is one.
AIC is \(2p-2\ell(\hat\beta)\); residual degrees of freedom are \(n-p\), without an estimated dispersion parameter. Predictions are mean counts, and residuals are observed minus fitted. These vectors follow retained input row order.

ll=log_likelihood(eta)
saturated=np.sum(xlogy(y,y)-y-gammaln(y+1))
model_deviance=2*(saturated-ll)
null_ll=np.sum(y*np.log(y.mean())-y.mean()-gammaln(y+1))
null_deviance=2*(saturated-null_ll)
print("Mean multipliers:",np.exp(beta))
print("Saturated log-likelihood:",saturated)
calculated=dict(coefficients=beta,covariance=covariance,std_errors=se,z_statistics=z,p_values=p_values,
                conf_int=conf_int,fitted=fitted,residuals=y-fitted,log_likelihood=ll,
                deviance=model_deviance,null_deviance=null_deviance,aic=2*p-2*ll,df_residual=n-p)
for key,value in calculated.items():
    np.testing.assert_allclose(value,case["expected"][key],atol=1e-9,rtol=1e-7,err_msg=key)

title: Poisson: count likelihood, log link and IRLS
text:
6. Assumptions, failure modes and experiments
Counts must be finite nonnegative integers and at least one must be positive. An all-zero sample is rejected, including no-intercept designs, as a conservative first-version restriction. Certain predictor patterns have a boundary MLE with coefficients diverging; the fitter rejects nonconvergence or singular information rather than returning a partial fit. It has no exhaustive boundary-existence test. Independent outcomes, equal conditional mean/variance and linear log mean are model assumptions. There are no offsets, exposures, sample weights, grouped trials, robust errors, zero-inflation or negative-binomial alternatives. Try doubling every count while retaining the design: which coefficient should shift, and why?
For both methods the retained design must have n > p and full numerical rank. Missing null/NAN rows are dropped with a warning unless missing: ‘raise’. No partial unconverged result is returned. See the contract and the executed three-way comparison.

title: Poisson: count likelihood, log link and IRLS
text:
Rust connections
fit_poisson owns its input vectors and converts them to nalgebra matrices. Borrowed matrix operands remain available for later iterations; iterators construct weights and score residuals. A dedicated loop performs this estimator’s updates. Result and ? propagate validation/numerical failures. The returned struct holds numeric fields; the PHP binding converts those fields into an associative array and adds warning/sample metadata. No generic optimizer or family hierarchy is added. See Rust learning notes and crates/stats-core/src/poisson.rs.
Reference documentation: R glm, R families, statsmodels GLM.

title: Ordinary least squares: from the objective to inference
text:
This is an executable companion to ols-math.qmd, for learning and reviewing the estimator. It uses Python to make the intermediate matrices visible; production estimation lives in crates/stats-core/src/ols.rs. NumPy and SciPy are notebook tools, not Rust dependencies. We use the same saved simulated housing observations as the PHP example and R fixtures. These are synthetic observations, not real housing records.
We model \(y=X\beta+\epsilon\). Rows are observations, columns are coefficients, and the first column is explicitly supplied ones. Our unknowns are the intercept and slope. We assume full column rank and \(n>p\). Run cells from top to bottom; see notebook setup.
from pathlib import Path
import json
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import t
from IPython.display import Math, display

def show_matrix(symbol, values):
    """Render calculated numbers as a LaTeX matrix, with its dimensions."""
    matrix = np.asarray(values)
    if matrix.ndim == 1:
        matrix = matrix[:, None]
    rows = [" & ".join(f"{value:.6g}" for value in row) for row in matrix]
    latex = r"\begin{bmatrix}" + r" \\ ".join(rows) + r"\end{bmatrix}"
    display(Math(symbol + " = " + latex + rf"\quad({matrix.shape[0]}\times {matrix.shape[1]})"))

def math_number(value):
    number = f"{value:.8g}"
    if "e" in number:
        mantissa, exponent = number.split("e")
        return mantissa + rf"\times10^{{{int(exponent)}}}"
    return number

def show_dot(symbol, left, right):
    """Show the first two and last products, but sum every term."""
    left, right = np.asarray(left), np.asarray(right)
    assert left.ndim == right.ndim == 1 and left.shape == right.shape
    terms = [rf"({math_number(a)})\cdot({math_number(b)})"
             for a, b in zip(left, right)]
    if len(terms) > 3:
        terms = terms[:2] + [r"\cdots", terms[-1]]
    display(Math(symbol + " = " + " + ".join(terms)
                 + r"\approx " + math_number(left @ right)))

title: Ordinary least squares: from the objective to inference
text:
1. What does fitting minimize?
For a candidate \(\beta\), fitted values are \(X\beta\) and residuals are \(r=y-X\beta\). The residual sum of squares is
\[RSS(\beta)=r^\top r=\sum_i(y_i-x_i^\top\beta)^2.\]
OLS chooses \(\hat\beta=\arg\min_\beta RSS(\beta)\). Squaring makes large errors costly and gives a smooth quadratic. Differentiating gives \(-2X^\top(y-X\beta)\); at the minimum,
\[X^\top X\hat\beta=X^\top y.\]
These normal equations explain the answer. Computing \((X^\top X)^{-1}\) directly is a poor numerical strategy: forming \(X^\top X\) squares the condition number. The implementation solves through SVD instead.

def rss_at(beta):
    residuals = y - X @ np.asarray(beta)
    return residuals @ residuals

print("RSS at generating coefficients [650, 18]:", rss_at([650, 18]))
print("Gradient there:", -2 * X.T @ (y - X @ np.array([650, 18])))

RSS at generating coefficients [650, 18]: 264940.4373000001
Gradient there: [  847.18  32810.806]


At the trial coefficients \(\beta=[650,18]^\top\), each fitted outcome is \(1\cdot650+\mathrm{area}_i\cdot18\). The residual is the observed outcome minus that fit.

trial_beta = np.array([650., 18.])
show_matrix(r"\beta_{\mathrm{trial}}", trial_beta)
show_matrix(r"X\beta_{\mathrm{trial}}", X @ trial_beta)
show_matrix(r"y-X\beta_{\mathrm{trial}}", y - X @ trial_beta)
show_matrix(r"X^\top X", X.T @ X)
show_matrix(r"X^\top y", X.T @ y)

Here \(X^\top X\) has dimensions \((2\times8)(8\times2)=2\times2\). Its top-left entry is the sum of eight squared ones, hence 8; its top-right entry is the sum of the observed floor areas; its bottom-right entry is the sum of their squares. For example, its top-right calculation begins \(1\cdot74.4+1\cdot57.4+\cdots+1\cdot93.9\). \(X^\top y\) contains the sum of rents and the sum of area–rent products. The normal equations give two equations for the two unknown coefficients. We show these products to understand the mathematics; the numerical solver below uses SVD rather than the normal equations.

Expand the dot products
Every entry in a matrix product is one row–column dot product. Below, we show the first two and last terms of long sums; \(\cdots\) stands for the omitted terms. The result includes all eight observations, not just the displayed terms. Both factors and results are rounded for display, so the equals sign describes the operation and \(\approx\) marks the displayed numerical result.

The subscripts here use mathematical indexing starting at 1 (Python indices start at 0). In particular, \((X^\top X)_{1,2}\) and \((X^\top X)_{2,1}\) are equal: swapping the two factors in every scalar product does not change their sum. This is why \(X^\top X\) is symmetric.

title: Ordinary least squares: from the objective to inference
section: 2. SVD gives a stable solution and a rank check
text:
2. SVD gives a stable solution and a rank check

What problem does SVD help us understand?
SVD means singular value decomposition. A decomposition rewrites one matrix as a product of simpler matrices. It does not change the data or guess the coefficients. For our model, multiplying \(X\beta\) takes two coefficient values and produces eight fitted rents. That is a map from a two-dimensional coefficient space into an eight-dimensional observation space.
The possible fitted vectors form the column space of \(X\): all linear combinations of its intercept and area columns. It is a two-dimensional plane through the origin inside that eight-dimensional space. The observed \(y\) will generally lie outside this plane because it includes noise. Least squares seeks the point on the plane closest to \(y\) in squared Euclidean distance.
These are spaces of vectors, not a scatterplot of area against rent: the eight coordinates of an observation-space vector correspond to the eight apartments.


Why scale the columns first?
Scale the columns with \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\|X_j\|)\), so \(A=XD^{-1}\). Decompose \(A=USV^\top\). Then
\[\hat\beta=D^{-1}VS^{-1}U^\top y.\]
The notation \(\|X_j\|=\sqrt{\sum_i X_{ij}^2}\) is the Euclidean length of column \(j\). \(D\) has those lengths on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Multiplying by \(D^{-1}\) divides each column by its length, giving unit-length columns in \(A\). This is column scaling, not centering or z-score standardization. The intercept column is scaled too; no observations are changed or removed.
Define scaled coefficients \(\theta=D\beta\). Then \(A\theta=X\beta\), so this change of units preserves every possible fitted vector. We solve for \(\theta\) and recover \(\beta=D^{-1}\theta\). Scaling prevents the numerical rank decision from being dominated simply by the choice of metres versus centimetres.


What do U, S and V mean?
For our full-rank design, the thin SVD is
\[A=USV^\top,\qquad
U^\top U=I_2,\qquad V^\top V=VV^\top=I_2.\]
\(I_2\) is the \(2\times2\) identity matrix: ones on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Orthonormal columns have length one and are perpendicular to one another; their dot products are therefore 1 with themselves and 0 with each other. Those equalities are exactly what the identity matrices say.








Matrix
Dimensions
Meaning




\(V\)
\(2\times2\)
Its columns \(v_j\) are orthonormal directions in scaled coefficient space. \(V^\top\) expresses a coefficient vector in those directions.


\(S\)
\(2\times2\)
Diagonal entries \(s_j\ge0\) are singular values: the amount that \(A\) stretches each corresponding direction.


\(U\)
\(8\times2\)
Its columns \(u_j\) are orthonormal directions spanning the possible fitted outcomes.



The key relationship for each direction is
\[A v_j=s_j u_j.\]
So an input direction \(v_j\) of length one becomes an output direction \(u_j\) stretched to length \(s_j\). Reading \(A\theta=USV^\top\theta\) right to left: change coordinates using \(V^\top\), scale them using \(S\), and combine the observation-space directions using \(U\). \(V^\top\) is a rotation or reflection; the rectangular \(U\) embeds two coordinates into the eight-dimensional fitted plane. The thin \(U\) is not an invertible \(8\times8\) rotation.
Singular values are not regression coefficients or error standard deviations. They describe the design matrix, independent of the observed rents \(y\).
If a singular value is numerically zero, at least one coefficient cannot be uniquely identified. We reject the design. The threshold is \(\epsilon\max(n,p)s_{max}\). Scaling makes this decision less dependent on predictor units. The Rust code calls nalgebra’s svd.solve() for the scaled solution, then undoes the column scaling.

scales = np.linalg.norm(X, axis=0)
A = X / scales
U, singular_values, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)
tolerance = np.finfo(float).eps * max(n, p) * singular_values[0]
assert np.all(singular_values > tolerance)
beta = (Vt.T @ ((U.T @ y) / singular_values)) / scales
print("Singular values:", singular_values)
print("Rank threshold:", tolerance)
print("Coefficients:", beta)
print("Normal-equation gradient (approximately zero):", -2 * X.T @ (y - X @ beta))

Coefficients: [372.47854453  21.47972428]

The thin SVD keeps only the \(p=2\) needed columns of \(U\). Here \(U\) is \(8\times2\), \(S\) is \(2\times2\), and \(V^\top\) is \(2\times2\). \(S\) is diagonal: its only nonzero entries are the singular values. \(D^{-1}\) undoes the original column scaling.

Check those geometric claims using the actual matrices:

show_matrix(r"U^\top U", U.T @ U)
show_matrix(r"V^\top V", Vt @ Vt.T)
show_matrix(r"Av_1", A @ Vt.T[:, 0])
show_matrix(r"s_1u_1", singular_values[0] * U[:, 0])
np.testing.assert_allclose(U.T @ U, np.eye(p), atol=1e-14)
np.testing.assert_allclose(Vt @ Vt.T, np.eye(p), atol=1e-14)
np.testing.assert_allclose(A @ Vt.T[:, 0], singular_values[0] * U[:, 0], atol=1e-14)

\(\displaystyle U^\top U = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1.40929e-17 \\ 1.40929e-17 & 1\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 2)\)


\(\displaystyle V^\top V = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times 2)\)


\(\displaystyle Av_1 = \begin{bmatrix}-0.525509 \\ -0.462557 \\ -0.495884 \\ -0.431821 \\ -0.419231 \\ -0.592164 \\ -0.387014 \\ -0.597719\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 1)\)


\(\displaystyle s_1u_1 = \begin{bmatrix}-0.525509 \\ -0.462557 \\ -0.495884 \\ -0.431821 \\ -0.419231 \\ -0.592164 \\ -0.387014 \\ -0.597719\end{bmatrix}\quad(8\times 1)\)




Derive the least-squares solution from the decomposition
First project the outcomes onto the columns of \(U\):
\[c=U^\top y,\qquad y_\parallel=Uc,\qquad
y_\perp=y-Uc.\]
Each \(c_j=u_j^\top y\) is a dot product measuring how much of \(y\) lies along direction \(u_j\). \(y_\parallel\) lies in the fitted plane, while \(y_\perp\) is perpendicular to it. The model can fit the first part; no choice of coefficients can reproduce the second part. This is a geometric decomposition of the observed sample, not recovery of the true simulation errors.
Write \(z=V^\top\theta\). Because the two residual components are perpendicular, the Pythagorean theorem gives
\[\|y-A\theta\|^2
=\|c-Sz\|^2+\|y_\perp\|^2.\]
The second term cannot change as we vary coefficients. The first term is minimized at zero by setting \(z_j=c_j/s_j\). Thus
\[\hat z=S^{-1}U^\top y,\qquad
\hat\theta=V\hat z,\qquad
\hat\beta=D^{-1}\hat\theta.\]
This explains the solution formula rather than just prescribing a sequence of matrix multiplications. It also gives \(\hat y=UU^\top y\) and \(r=y-UU^\top y\). \(UU^\top\) is a projection matrix, not the \(8\times8\) identity: it preserves vectors in the fitted plane and removes perpendicular components. There are two fitted directions and six residual directions, which is where \(n-p=8-2=6\) comes from.

coordinates = U.T @ y
projected_y = U @ coordinates
perpendicular_y = y - projected_y

Reading the final product from right to left: \(U^\top y\) expresses the outcome in the left singular-vector directions; \(S^{-1}\) divides by the singular values; \(V\) converts back to scaled coefficient coordinates; \(D^{-1}\) restores the original predictor units. Each intermediate coefficient vector is \(2\times1\). The signs of corresponding singular vectors can differ across software while giving the same reconstructed matrix and coefficients.

\(S^{-1}\) and \(D^{-1}\) are diagonal, so multiplying by them simply divides each coordinate by its corresponding singular value or column scale.


Why small singular values matter
If \(s_j=0\), then \(Av_j=0\): moving the coefficients along that nonzero direction does not change any fitted outcome. The data cannot distinguish those coefficient choices. For example, adding a second copy of area lets one area coefficient increase while the other decreases by the same amount. Only their sum matters.
If \(s_j\) is small but positive, division by \(s_j\) amplifies changes in the outcome coordinates. The design is identifiable but coefficients can be sensitive to noise. The condition number \(\kappa(A)=s_{\max}/s_{\min}\) measures that sensitivity in the scaled coordinates. Strongly correlated predictors often produce small singular values; full rank alone does not guarantee precise estimates.

print("Condition number of scaled design:", singular_values[0] / singular_values[-1])
duplicated = np.column_stack([X, X[:, 1]])
duplicated_scaled = duplicated / np.linalg.norm(duplicated, axis=0)
duplicate_singular_values = np.linalg.svd(duplicated_scaled, compute_uv=False)
duplicate_threshold = (np.finfo(float).eps * max(duplicated.shape)
                       * duplicate_singular_values[0])
show_matrix(r"\text{singular values with duplicated area}", duplicate_singular_values)
print("Smallest value:", duplicate_singular_values[-1])
print("Numerical rank threshold:", duplicate_threshold)
assert duplicate_singular_values[-1] <= duplicate_threshold

Numerical rank threshold: 3.0465504588638278e-15


In floating-point arithmetic, an exact zero may appear as a tiny positive number. Our threshold treats such directions as numerically rank deficient and rejects the fit with a clear error. It does not silently discard a predictor or divide by a nearly zero value.
Finally, \(A^\top A=VS^2V^\top\), so forming the normal-equation matrix squares the singular values and its condition number is \(\kappa(A)^2\). This can lose accuracy before a solve even begins. SVD works with \(A\) directly and exposes its rank. It avoids that extra numerical damage; it cannot make redundant predictors identifiable or make noisy data informative.

3. Residuals and degrees of freedom
Full rank means we estimate \(p\) coefficients, leaving \(n-p\) independent residual directions. The unbiased variance estimate is
\[s^2=\frac{RSS}{n-p},\qquad s=\sqrt{s^2}.\]
The result fields are fitted, residuals, rss, df_residual, residual_variance, and sigma. We preserve actual floating-point residuals; we do not round nearly perfect fits to zero.

title: Ordinary least squares: from the objective to inference
text:
4. Covariance, standard errors and t-tests
Under independent errors with constant variance,
\[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)=s^2(X^\top X)^{-1}
=s^2D^{-1}VS^{-2}V^\top D^{-1}.\]
The code computes the latter expression, without forming \(X^\top X\). Standard errors are the square roots of the diagonal. Under Gaussian errors, \((\hat\beta_j-\beta_j)/SE_j\) has a Student t distribution with \(n-p\) degrees of freedom. For \(H_0:\beta_j=0\), the statistic is \(t_j=\hat\beta_j/SE_j\), the two-sided p-value is \(2P(T\ge |t_j|)\), and the 95% interval is \(\hat\beta_j\pm t_{0.975,n-p}SE_j\).
Use the survival function for upper tails to avoid subtracting a CDF close to one. These are conventional homoskedastic standard errors, not robust estimates.
For the fixed 95% interval, Rust finds the critical value by bisection on \(P(T>t)=0.025\). Large-sample checks found that statrs’ inverse-beta quantile lost precision at high residual degrees of freedom. Solving on the survival function preserves agreement with R; this notebook independently uses SciPy’s t.ppf. See the large-data report and the focused Rust critical-value test for the regression evidence.

scaled_inverse = (Vt.T / singular_values) @ (Vt / singular_values[:, None])
covariance = variance * scaled_inverse / scales[:, None] / scales[None, :]
se = np.sqrt(np.diag(covariance))
t_statistics = beta / se
p_values = 2 * t.sf(np.abs(t_statistics), df)
critical = t.ppf(0.975, df)
conf_int = np.column_stack([beta - critical * se, beta + critical * se])
display(pd.DataFrame(covariance, index=["intercept", "area_m2"], columns=["intercept", "area_m2"]))
display(pd.DataFrame({"coefficient": beta, "SE": se, "t": t_statistics, "p": p_values,
                      "lower 95%": conf_int[:, 0], "upper 95%": conf_int[:, 1]}, index=["intercept", "area_m2"]))

title: Ordinary least squares: from the objective to inference
text:
5. R-squared and the intercept convention
With a column of exact ones, use \(TSS=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2\) and \(R^2=1-RSS/TSS\). Adjusted R-squared is \(1-(1-R^2)(n-1)/(n-p)\).
Without an intercept, use uncentered \(TSS=\sum_i y_i^2\) and adjusted R-squared \(1-(1-R^2)n/(n-p)\), matching R’s no-intercept convention. Do not compare centered and uncentered R-squared as if they used the same baseline.

has_intercept = bool(np.any(np.all(X == 1, axis=0)))
tss = np.sum((y - y.mean()) ** 2) if has_intercept else y @ y
r_squared = 1 - rss / tss
adj_r_squared = 1 - (1 - r_squared) * (n - int(has_intercept)) / df
print(f"R²={r_squared:.9f}; adjusted R²={adj_r_squared:.9f}")

title: Ordinary least squares: from the objective to inference
section: 6. Gaussian likelihood explains the same estimator
text:
6. Gaussian likelihood explains the same estimator
For independent \(y_i\sim N(x_i^\top\beta,\sigma^2)\), multiply the normal densities and take logs:
\[\ell(\beta,\sigma^2)=-\frac n2\log(2\pi\sigma^2)-\frac{RSS(\beta)}{2\sigma^2}.\]
At fixed positive variance, maximizing this expression minimizes RSS, so it gives the same OLS coefficients. Differentiate with respect to \(v=\sigma^2\):
\[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial v}=-\frac{n}{2v}+\frac{RSS}{2v^2}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\hat v_{ML}=RSS/n.\]
This ML variance differs from \(RSS/(n-p)\) used for standard errors. At the estimates,
\[\ell(\hat\beta,\hat v_{ML})=-\frac n2[\log(2\pi)+\log(RSS/n)+1].\]

ml_variance = rss / n
log_likelihood = -n / 2 * (np.log(2 * np.pi) + np.log(ml_variance) + 1)
def log_likelihood_at(candidate, v):
    return -n / 2 * np.log(2 * np.pi * v) - rss_at(candidate) / (2 * v)
print(f"ML variance={ml_variance:.8f}; inference variance={variance:.8f}")
print(f"Log-likelihood={log_likelihood:.9f}")
assert log_likelihood_at(beta, ml_variance) > log_likelihood_at(beta + [0, 0.1], ml_variance)
assert log_likelihood_at(beta, ml_variance) > log_likelihood_at(beta, 2 * ml_variance)

7. Verify what we calculated
These checks compare the independently displayed steps to the committed R reference. The three implementation notebook executes R, statsmodels and the PHP extension on the same data and checks every returned statistical field. Cross-implementation agreement is evidence; it does not replace understanding the formulas.

                  t_statistics=t_statistics, p_values=p_values, conf_int=conf_int,
                  fitted=fitted, residuals=residuals, rss=rss, residual_variance=variance,
                  sigma=sigma, r_squared=r_squared, adj_r_squared=adj_r_squared,
                  df_residual=df, log_likelihood=log_likelihood)
for key, value in calculated.items():
    np.testing.assert_allclose(value, case["expected"][key], atol=1e-9, rtol=1e-7, err_msg=key)
print("All displayed calculations agree with the committed R fixture.")

All displayed calculations agree with the committed R fixture.

title: Ordinary least squares: from the objective to inference
section: 8. Missing data, singularity and perfect fits
text:
8. Missing data, singularity and perfect fits
The PHP call drops a whole row if any supplied predictor or its outcome is null or NAN, warns once on a successful fit, and reports original row positions. It applies all formulas above to the retained sample: \(n\) and \(n-p\) change. Use missing: 'raise' to reject missingness. Infinity, malformed values and rank failure remain errors. See missing-data contract.
Listwise deletion changes the estimation sample; it is not imputation and does not guarantee unbiased results when missingness is related to the outcome or predictors. Document why data are missing and which observations were retained.
At exact zero RSS, standard errors are zero and the Gaussian log-likelihood has an infinite limit as variance approaches zero. A zero coefficient divided by a zero standard error is undefined (NaN); a nonzero coefficient gives infinite t and zero p. If TSS is also zero, R-squared is undefined. Decomposition roundoff can leave small residuals in mathematically perfect fits; unstable t-statistics and likelihoods should not be compared tightly across algorithms.

The model uses marginal maximum likelihood, a logit link and a Gaussian random intercept. Inputs remain plain design/outcome/group arrays. See the math walkthrough and contract.
