title: Binomial mixed-model verification and approximation accuracy
text:
Numerical tolerance and failure policy

Estimates/predictions/group modes: absolute 2e-5 plus relative 2e-4.
Covariance, standard errors, z tests, p-values and intervals: absolute 2e-5 plus relative 2e-3; R and native use independently computed finite-difference Hessians.
Likelihood/AIC/BIC: absolute 1e-6 plus relative 1e-8.
Independent matched-approximation likelihood: absolute 2e-8.
Sample metadata, group ordering, integer counts and singular flags are exact where checked. Boundary reduction also checks equality with the native GLM.

The coefficient covariance is the fixed block of inverse joint marginal observed information, including scale coupling. A nonpositive Hessian, excessive final score, invalid/aliased design, fixed separation, invalid counts or exhausted budget throws an error. Controls have explicit parameter bounds; convergence is local and does not prove global optimality. Missingness follows the existing listwise policy with one warning and original retained/dropped positions.

title: Binary logistic regression: from probabilities to maximum likelihood
text: This executable walkthrough uses saved simulated students, not real student records. It derives the Bernoulli likelihood, shows the matrices and dot products, and follows Newton/IRLS iterations to the result returned by stats_logistic(). Production calculations live in crates/stats-core/src/logistic.rs; Python here makes the intermediate values visible. See setup.

title: Binary logistic regression: from probabilities to maximum likelihood
text:
1. Observations, parameters and probabilities
Each observation has study hours, a practice score and an observed pass/fail outcome. Those input values are data, not coefficient guesses. The supplied column of ones is constructed to estimate an intercept. We simulate 80 students using R seed 20261012, with practice scores correlated with study hours:
\[\mathrm{score}_i=\operatorname{clip}(45+3\,\mathrm{hours}_i+e_i,20,95),
\qquad e_i\sim N(0,8^2).\]
Hours are uniform between 1 and 12; hours and scores are rounded to two decimals. The true generating coefficients are \([-3.28,0.22,0.018]^\top\):
\[\eta_i=-3.28+0.22\,\mathrm{hours}_i+0.018\,\mathrm{score}_i,
\qquad \pi_i=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta_i}},\qquad y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i).\]
A Bernoulli outcome is either 0 or 1. A probability such as 0.6 means a 60% chance of success under the model; the observed outcome is still a single 0 or 1. The generator is tests/generate-logistic-fixtures.R; the shared observations are in learning.csv. Known generating coefficients and estimated coefficients are different objects: estimates vary with the random sample.

from pathlib import Path
import json
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.special import expit
from scipy.stats import norm
from IPython.display import Math, display

ROOT = next(p for p in [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents] if (p / "Cargo.toml").exists())
observations = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "docs/data/learning.csv")
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(observations)), observations[["study_hours", "practice_score"]]])
y = observations["passed"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
n, p = X.shape
fixture = json.loads((ROOT / "tests/fixtures/logistic-r.json").read_text())
case = next(c for c in fixture["cases"] if c["name"] == "simulated_learning")
np.testing.assert_array_equal(X, case["x"])
np.testing.assert_array_equal(y, case["y"])
display(observations.head(8))
display(observations.corr().rename_axis("Sample Pearson correlations"))
print("Observed successes:", int(y.sum()), "of", n)

def number(value):
    text = f"{value:.6g}"
    if "e" in text:
        mantissa, exponent = text.split("e")
        return mantissa + rf"\times10^{{{int(exponent)}}}"
    return text

def show_matrix(symbol, values, limit=6):
    matrix = np.asarray(values)
    if matrix.ndim == 1:
        matrix = matrix[:, None]
    indices = list(range(len(matrix))) if len(matrix) <= limit else [0,1,2,None,len(matrix)-1]
    columns = list(range(matrix.shape[1])) if matrix.shape[1] <= limit else [0,1,2,None,matrix.shape[1]-1]
    rows = [" & ".join(r"\ddots" if j is None else r"\vdots" for j in columns) if i is None
            else " & ".join(r"\cdots" if j is None else number(matrix[i,j]) for j in columns) for i in indices]
    display(Math(symbol + r"=\begin{bmatrix}" + r" \\ ".join(rows)
                 + r"\end{bmatrix}" + rf"\quad({matrix.shape[0]}\times{matrix.shape[1]})"))

def show_dot(symbol, left, right):
    terms = [rf"({number(a)})\cdot({number(b)})" for a,b in zip(left,right)]
    if len(terms) > 3:
        terms = terms[:2] + [r"\cdots", terms[-1]]
    display(Math(symbol + "=" + "+".join(terms) + r"\approx" + number(np.asarray(left) @ right)))

title: Binary logistic regression: from probabilities to maximum likelihood
section: 2. Why model log-odds instead of the outcome directly?
text:
2. Why model log-odds instead of the outcome directly?
OLS can produce fitted values outside \([0,1]\). Here the linear predictor \(\eta_i=x_i^\top\beta\) is mapped through the sigmoid, so \(0<\pi_i<1\) in exact arithmetic. Rearranging gives
\[\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}=e^{\eta_i},\qquad
\log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}=x_i^\top\beta.\]
The fraction is the odds, while its logarithm is the logit. A probability of 0.75 gives odds \(0.75/0.25=3\): three successes per failure in the model’s long-run proportions. Holding other predictors fixed, increasing predictor \(j\) by one unit adds \(\beta_j\) to log-odds and multiplies odds by \(e^{\beta_j}\). It does not add a fixed amount to probability.

true_beta = np.array([-3.28, 0.22, 0.018])
show_dot(r"\eta_1\text{ at generating coefficients}", X[0], true_beta)

                      "generating probability": expit(-3.28+0.22*np.array([2,6,10])+0.018*65)}))
print("Generating odds multiplier for one additional study hour:", np.exp(0.22))

title: Binary logistic regression: from probabilities to maximum likelihood
text:
3. Write the likelihood
For one independent Bernoulli observation,
\[P(y_i\mid x_i,\beta)=\pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i}.\]
If \(y_i=1\), its likelihood contribution is \(\pi_i\); if \(y_i=0\), it is \(1-\pi_i\). Multiply contributions across students and take logs:
\[\ell(\beta)=\sum_i\left[y_i\log\pi_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-\pi_i)\right]
=\sum_i\left[y_i\eta_i-\log(1+e^{\eta_i})\right].\]
We maximize this likelihood, rather than minimize squared outcome errors. There is no separate Gaussian error variance: the Bernoulli variance is \(\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\). Dispersion is fixed at 1.
Naively evaluating exponentials can overflow. Rust uses a stable sigmoid and \(\operatorname{softplus}(a)=\max(a,0)+\log(1+e^{-|a|})\); a success contributes \(-\operatorname{softplus}(-\eta_i)\) and a failure contributes \(-\operatorname{softplus}(\eta_i)\). These expressions also avoid cancellation.

def log_likelihood(beta):
    eta = X @ beta
    return -np.logaddexp(0, np.where(y == 1, -eta, eta)).sum()

initial_beta = np.zeros(p)
initial_eta = X @ initial_beta
initial_prob = expit(initial_eta)
show_matrix(r"\beta^{(0)}", initial_beta)
show_matrix(r"\pi^{(0)}", initial_prob)
print("Initial log-likelihood:", log_likelihood(initial_beta))
print("At generating coefficients:", log_likelihood(true_beta))

Zero initial coefficients are starting guesses. They imply probability 0.5 for every student. They are distinct from the observed \(X\) and \(y\).

title: Binary logistic regression: from probabilities to maximum likelihood
text:
4. Derivatives give the Newton step
For one row, write \(\ell_i=y_i\eta_i-\log(1+e^{\eta_i})\). The derivative with respect to \(\eta_i\) is \(y_i-\pi_i\), because \(d\log(1+e^{\eta_i})/d\eta_i=\pi_i\). Also \(d\eta_i/d\beta_j=x_{ij}\). The chain rule therefore gives
\[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta_j}=\sum_i x_{ij}(y_i-\pi_i).\]
Differentiate again using \(d\pi_i/d\eta_i=\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\):
\[\frac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial\beta_j\partial\beta_k}
=-\sum_i x_{ij}\pi_i(1-\pi_i)x_{ik}.\]
These sums are exactly the dot products in the matrix score (gradient) and Hessian:
\[g=X^\top(y-\pi),\qquad H=-X^\top W X,
\qquad W=\operatorname{diag}\{\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\}.\]
\(g\) is \(3\times1\); \(H\) is \(3\times3\); \(W\) is an \(80\times80\) diagonal matrix. The negative Hessian \(I=X^\top W X\) is the information matrix. It is positive definite for an identifiable finite fit, making the log-likelihood concave. Newton’s method solves
\[I\,\Delta\beta=g,\qquad \beta_{\mathrm{next}}=\beta+\Delta\beta.\]
We show the information matrix to understand the arithmetic, but the production solver avoids forming/inverting it. It scales columns just as OLS does, then solves a weighted least-squares problem using SVD.

initial_residual = y-initial_prob
initial_weights = initial_prob*(1-initial_prob)
gradient = X.T @ initial_residual
information = X.T @ (initial_weights[:,None]*X)
show_matrix(r"y-\pi^{(0)}", initial_residual)
show_matrix(r"W^{(0)}_{1:5,1:5}\text{ (top-left block)}", np.diag(initial_weights[:5]))
show_matrix(r"g^{(0)}=X^\top(y-\pi^{(0)})", gradient)
show_matrix(r"I^{(0)}=X^\top W^{(0)}X", information)
for j in range(p):
    show_dot(rf"g_{{{j+1}}}", X[:,j], initial_residual)
show_dot(r"I_{2,3}", X[:,1], initial_weights*X[:,2])

\(\displaystyle W^{(0)}_{1:5,1:5}\text{ (top-left block)}=\begin{bmatrix}0.25 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.25 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.25 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0.25\end{bmatrix}\quad(5\times5)\)

\(\displaystyle I_{2,3}=(8.2)\cdot(17.42)+(3.77)\cdot(13.5125)+\cdots+(2.08)\cdot(11.2775)\approx8291.44\)


At the start, every weight is \(0.5(1-0.5)=0.25\). The gradient’s first entry sums observed minus predicted successes. Its other entries weight those differences by hours or practice scores. \(I_{2,3}\) is a weighted dot product of the two predictor columns. Subscripts in the equations start at 1.

title: Binary logistic regression: from probabilities to maximum likelihood
section: 5. Weighted SVD, IRLS and step halving
text:
5. Weighted SVD, IRLS and step halving
Let \(D\) contain column lengths, \(A=XD^{-1}\) and \(\theta=D\beta\). The Newton increment is the least-squares solution to
\[B\Delta\theta\approx q,\qquad B=W^{1/2}A,
\qquad q=W^{-1/2}(y-\pi).\]
Taking its normal equations produces \(A^\top W A\Delta\theta=A^\top(y-\pi)\), the scaled Newton equation. For \(B=USV^\top\) we get \(\Delta\theta=VS^{-1}U^\top q\), then \(\Delta\beta=D^{-1}\Delta\theta\). See the SVD explanation for the geometry of these factors.
This is iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS): probabilities and weights change after each fit. Equivalently, a working response \(z_i=\eta_i+(y_i-\pi_i)/w_i\), where \(w_i=\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\), is fitted using weighted least squares. We solve for the increment directly to avoid unnecessarily large working-response values.

scales = np.linalg.norm(X, axis=0)
A = X/scales
theta = np.zeros(p)
history = []
for iteration in range(1,101):
    eta = A @ theta
    probability = expit(eta)
    exponential = np.exp(-np.abs(eta))
    root_weights = np.sqrt(exponential)/(1+exponential)
    score_residual = np.where(y == 1, expit(-eta), -expit(eta))
    B = root_weights[:,None]*A
    q = score_residual/root_weights
    U, singular_values, Vt = np.linalg.svd(B, full_matrices=False)
    assert np.all(singular_values > np.finfo(float).eps*max(n,p)*singular_values[0])
    step = Vt.T @ ((U.T @ q)/singular_values)
    old_ll = log_likelihood(theta/scales)
    fraction = 1.0
    for _ in range(31):
        candidate = theta+fraction*step
        new_ll = log_likelihood(candidate/scales)
        if new_ll >= old_ll-16*np.finfo(float).eps*(1+abs(old_ll)):
            break
        fraction /= 2
    else:
        raise RuntimeError("No improving Newton step")
    if iteration == 1:
        show_matrix(r"B^{(0)}=W^{1/2}A",B)
        show_matrix(r"q^{(0)}=W^{-1/2}(y-\pi)",q)
        show_matrix(r"U^\top q",U.T @ q)
        show_matrix(r"\Delta\theta",step)
        show_matrix(r"\Delta\beta=D^{-1}\Delta\theta",step/scales)
        np.testing.assert_allclose(information @ (step/scales),gradient,atol=1e-10)
    history.append({"iteration":iteration,"step fraction":fraction,"log-likelihood":new_ll,
                    "intercept":candidate[0]/scales[0],"hours coefficient":candidate[1]/scales[1],
                    "score coefficient":candidate[2]/scales[2],"largest full scaled step":np.max(np.abs(step))})
    small_step = np.all(np.abs(step) <= 1e-8*(1+np.abs(candidate)))
    small_ll = abs(new_ll-old_ll) <= 1e-10*(1+abs(old_ll))
    theta = candidate
    if small_step and small_ll:
        break
else:
    raise RuntimeError("Not converged")
beta = theta/scales
display(pd.DataFrame(history))
show_matrix(r"\hat\beta",beta)
assert np.all(np.diff([row["log-likelihood"] for row in history]) >= -1e-10)

title: Binary logistic regression: from probabilities to maximum likelihood
text:
6. Probabilities, residuals and uncertainty
The fitted outputs are \(\hat\pi=\operatorname{sigmoid}(X\hat\beta)\), not labels obtained by a 0.5 threshold. Response residuals are \(y-\hat\pi\). For conventional maximum-likelihood inference,
\[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)=(X^\top\hat W X)^{-1},
\qquad \operatorname{SE}_j=\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)_{jj}}.\]
Information is recalculated at the final estimate. There is no multiplication by \(\mathrm{RSS}/(n-p)\). Large-sample Wald inference uses
\[z_j=\hat\beta_j/\operatorname{SE}_j,\qquad
p_j=2P(Z\ge|z_j|),\qquad
\operatorname{CI}_{95\%,j}=\hat\beta_j\pm1.959964\,\operatorname{SE}_j.\]
Here \(Z\) is standard normal: these are asymptotic z-tests, not the exact Gaussian t-tests used for OLS. Sparse outcomes or near-separation can make Wald inference unreliable even if a finite fit exists. Coefficient intervals are on the log-odds scale; exponentiating their endpoints gives Wald intervals for odds ratios.

eta = X @ beta
fitted = expit(eta)
residuals = y-fitted
exponential = np.exp(-np.abs(eta))
root_weights = np.sqrt(exponential)/(1+exponential)
_, singular_values, Vt = np.linalg.svd(root_weights[:,None]*A,full_matrices=False)
inverse = (Vt.T/singular_values) @ (Vt/singular_values[:,None])
covariance = inverse/scales[:,None]/scales[None,:]
se = np.sqrt(np.diag(covariance))
z_statistics = beta/se
p_values = 2*norm.sf(np.abs(z_statistics))
conf_int = np.column_stack([beta-norm.ppf(.975)*se,beta+norm.ppf(.975)*se])
show_matrix(r"\hat\pi",fitted)

title: Binary logistic regression: from probabilities to maximum likelihood
text:
7. Likelihood, deviance and AIC
For individual binary observations, the saturated model fits every outcome with probability 0 or 1 and has limiting log-likelihood zero. Thus
\[D=-2\ell(\hat\beta),\qquad \mathrm{AIC}=2p-2\ell(\hat\beta).\]
With an explicit ones column, the null model estimates a constant probability \(\bar y\). Without that column, our null convention has no coefficients and fixed probability 0.5. null_deviance is minus twice that null log-likelihood. df_residual is \(n-p\), but it is not used to estimate a Bernoulli dispersion or select a t distribution. The result intentionally has no OLS R-squared or sigma.

ll = log_likelihood(beta)
null_ll = np.sum(y*np.log(y.mean())+(1-y)*np.log1p(-y.mean()))
calculated = dict(coefficients=beta,covariance=covariance,std_errors=se,z_statistics=z_statistics,
                  p_values=p_values,conf_int=conf_int,fitted=fitted,residuals=residuals,
                  log_likelihood=ll,deviance=-2*ll,null_deviance=-2*null_ll,aic=2*p-2*ll,df_residual=n-p)
for key,value in calculated.items():
    np.testing.assert_allclose(value,case["expected"][key],atol=1e-9,rtol=1e-7,err_msg=key)
print({key:calculated[key] for key in ["log_likelihood","deviance","null_deviance","aic","df_residual"]})
print("Every displayed statistical result agrees with the committed R fixture.")

title: Binary logistic regression: from probabilities to maximum likelihood
section: 8. Separation, assumptions and things to try
text:
8. Separation, assumptions and things to try
If a predictor combination puts every success on one side and every failure on the other, coefficients can grow without bound while likelihood improves. This is complete separation: there is no finite unpenalized MLE. Quasi-complete separation allows some observations on the boundary. The implementation checks whether an encountered coefficient vector certifies separation; it also rejects rank-deficient information and iteration exhaustion. It is not an exhaustive linear-programming separation detector and does not guarantee detection of every numerically difficult case. It never returns a converged: false partial fit.
This first version requires both classes, finite full-rank inputs, and \(n>p\). It supports individual 0/1 outcomes only: no grouped trials, sample weights, penalties, Firth correction, or automatic threshold selection. The model assumes independent observations and linear log-odds in the supplied predictors. Missing-data deletion occurs before estimation and warns as in OLS; see the contract.
Try predicting the result before changing the notebook: set all outcomes to 1; replace the outcome by study_hours > 6; duplicate a predictor; convert hours to minutes; or remove the ones column. Which change causes an error, changes the meaning of a coefficient, or changes the null model? Comparing these cases is a way to connect estimation, identifiability and units.

title: Binary logistic regression: from probabilities to maximum likelihood
text:
Rust connections
fit_logistic takes ownership of Vec<Vec<f64>> and Vec<f64>, then converts them into nalgebra’s dynamic DMatrix and DVector. The matrix constructor explicitly reads the supplied row order; nalgebra stores its matrix internally by columns. Expressions such as &scaled * &candidate borrow those matrices for an operation so subsequent iterations can reuse them. Iterators build weights, score residuals and output vectors without PHP types entering the core.
LogisticResult is a struct holding the complete fit. Result<LogisticResult, StatsError> makes unsuccessful estimation explicit; the ? operator propagates failed decomposition or line-search operations. There is no mutable model object or general optimizer interface. The dedicated loop updates trial coefficients, checks progress, then recomputes information at the accepted final coefficients.
The binding validates PHP integer/float values, removes missing rows according to policy, calls this owned Rust function, and inserts its vectors and scalars into a PHP associative array. Core errors become PHP exceptions, and deletion produces a warning with row metadata. See the OLS Rust learning notes for more explanation of the shared language constructs.
Sources: R glm, R summary.glm, separation and finite estimates.

title: Gaussian mixed models on four published datasets
text:
We verify the optimized random-intercept ML implementation on four published datasets, in addition to the synthetic fixtures, closed-form variance test and million-row benchmarks. Every model uses the same explicit fixed columns and observations in R lme4, R nlme, Python statsmodels and PHP. Data provenance, original research references, CSV downloads and checksums are in the data-source record.
These are numerical comparisons of the specified models. They do not establish that a random intercept adequately models each scientific study. In particular, we do not reproduce the random-slope sleepstudy example or a worker-by-machine interaction. All fits are marginal maximum likelihood, not REML.

title: Gaussian random slopes, penalized least squares and REML
text: The random-intercept walkthrough introduces clustering. Here we allow each subject both a different starting reaction time and a different response to days of sleep deprivation. We use the published sleepstudy data, not synthetic row numbers. The optimizer audit verifies this model against R lme4 and statsmodels under ML and REML.

title: Gaussian random slopes, penalized least squares and REML
text:
Observations and matrices
\[
y_i=o_i+x_i^\top\beta+z_i^\top b_{g(i)}+\epsilon_i,
\qquad b_g\sim N(0,\Sigma),\quad
\epsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2/w_i).
\]
Here o is a known offset, w is a positive prior weight, x contains fixed predictors and z contains random predictors. For sleepstudy, o=0, w=1 and both local designs have [1, Days] columns. The ones construct an intercept; Days is observed data. Beta contains the population intercept and slope. Each group’s b contains deviations from those population coefficients, not a second set of observed predictors.

title: Gaussian random slopes, penalized least squares and REML
text:
Covariance through a Cholesky factor
Instead of optimizing variance/correlation entries directly, optimize a lower triangular relative factor:
\[
L=\begin{bmatrix}a&0\\c&d\end{bmatrix},\qquad a,d\geq0,
\qquad\Sigma=\sigma^2LL^\top
=\sigma^2\begin{bmatrix}a^2&ac\\ac&c^2+d^2\end{bmatrix}.
\]
This guarantees positive semidefinite covariance, including valid zero-variance or perfect-correlation boundaries. A negative c can represent negative intercept/slope covariance. lme4’s lower-triangle parameter ordering is column-major: [a, c, d]. Several terms concatenate their parameters in supplied term order.

from scipy.linalg import cholesky
reference=c['references']['bobyqa']['result']
Sigma=np.array(reference['terms'][0]['covariance'])
sigma2=reference['residual_variance'];L=cholesky(Sigma/sigma2,lower=True)
matrix_tex(L,'L');matrix_tex(sigma2*L@L.T,r'\widehat\Sigma')
print('Intercept SD (ms):',np.sqrt(Sigma[0,0]))
print('Slope SD (ms/day):',np.sqrt(Sigma[1,1]))
print('Intercept/slope correlation:',Sigma[0,1]/np.sqrt(Sigma[0,0]*Sigma[1,1]))

\(\displaystyle L=\begin{bmatrix}0.96673 & 0 \\ 0.015169 & 0.23091\end{bmatrix}\)


\(\displaystyle \widehat\Sigma=\begin{bmatrix}612.09 & 9.6043 \\ 9.6043 & 35.072\end{bmatrix}\)


Intercept SD (ms): 24.740448320046763
Slope SD (ms/day): 5.922133032515655
Intercept/slope correlation: 0.06555126695736169


These are estimated quantities from the full sample. They are not initial guesses. The off-diagonal dot product a*c + 0*d produces the covariance after multiplying by sigma². Variances have different physical units because the second coefficient is measured in milliseconds per day.

title: Gaussian random slopes, penalized least squares and REML
section: Penalized least squares profiles out beta and random effects
text:
Penalized least squares profiles out beta and random effects
Repeat L once per group to construct block-diagonal Lambda. Write b=Lambda u, where u has spherical covariance sigma²I. Given theta, minimize
\[
q(\theta)=\min_{u,\beta}
\left\|W^{1/2}(y-o-X\beta-Z\Lambda u)\right\|^2+\|u\|^2.
\]
The first term fits observed reaction times; the second penalizes implausibly large standardized random effects. This is a consequence of their Gaussian likelihood, not an arbitrary regularization parameter chosen by the user. It is the least-squares problem
\[
\begin{bmatrix}W^{1/2}Z\Lambda&W^{1/2}X\\I&0\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}u\\\beta\end{bmatrix}
\approx\begin{bmatrix}W^{1/2}(y-o)\\0\end{bmatrix}.
\]
For a selected theta, linear algebra finds u and beta. The nonlinear optimizer searches theta only. We solve with QR; coefficients do not come from explicitly inverting a normal-equation matrix.

from scipy.linalg import block_diag,solve_triangular
Lambda=block_diag(*([L]*len(order)))
A=np.block([[Z@Lambda,x],[np.eye(Z.shape[1]),np.zeros((Z.shape[1],x.shape[1]))]])
b=np.r_[y,np.zeros(Z.shape[1])]
Q,R=np.linalg.qr(A,mode='reduced');solution=solve_triangular(R,Q.T@b)
u=solution[:Z.shape[1]];beta=solution[Z.shape[1]:];effects=Lambda@u
residual=y-x@beta-Z@effects
q=residual@residual+u@u
print('Augmented design:',A.shape)
print('beta:',beta)
print('Observation residual contribution:',residual@residual)
print('Random-effect penalty contribution:',u@u)
print('Total profiled q:',q)
assert np.allclose(beta,reference['coefficients'],rtol=1e-8,atol=1e-8)
assert np.allclose(effects.reshape(-1,2),reference['terms'][0]['effects'],rtol=1e-8,atol=1e-8)

Augmented design: (216, 38)
beta: [251.40510485  10.46728596]
Observation residual contribution: 98881.64284605399
Random-effect penalty contribution: 17697.86289393207
Total profiled q: 116579.50573998605


The code uses an additional QR compression before optimization. QR of weighted [Z, X/scales, y-offset] preserves every trial residual norm. Each trial needs only that compact square-root summary plus identity penalty rows. This extends the earlier cached random-intercept idea. The current general summary is dense; lme4 uses sparse factorization to support larger random designs.

title: Gaussian random slopes, penalized least squares and REML
section: ML and REML are different objectives
text:
ML and REML are different objectives
With C=W⁻¹+Z Lambda Lambdaᵀ Zᵀ, the profiled Gaussian ML scale is
\[\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=q/n.\]
The negative profiled marginal log-likelihood is
\[
-\ell_{ML}(\theta)=\tfrac12\left[
n\{\log(2\pi)+1+\log(q/n)\}+\log|C|
\right].
\]
REML adjusts for estimating the p fixed coefficients. It uses
\[
\hat\sigma^2_{REML}=q/(n-p),
\]
and the restricted criterion
\[
-\ell_{REML}(\theta)=\tfrac12\left[
(n-p)\{\log(2\pi)+1+\log(q/(n-p))\}
+\log|C|+\log|X^\top C^{-1}X|
\right].
\]
REML changes the optimization objective, not merely the final denominator. Its extra determinant accounts for fixed-effect estimation. Both determinants come from triangular QR factors in our implementation. Scaling fixed columns requires restoring their determinant contribution, even though scaling does not change the fitted mean. REML likelihood values should not compare different fixed-effect designs.

qr_random=R[:Z.shape[1],:Z.shape[1]]
qr_fixed=R[Z.shape[1]:,Z.shape[1]:]
logdet_C=2*np.log(abs(np.diag(qr_random))).sum()
logdet_info=2*np.log(abs(np.diag(qr_fixed))).sum()
df=len(y)-x.shape[1]
reml_variance=q/df
reml_ll=-.5*(df*(np.log(2*np.pi)+1+np.log(reml_variance))+logdet_C+logdet_info)
print('n, p, n-p:',len(y),x.shape[1],df)
print('q/(n-p):',reml_variance)
print('log determinant C:',logdet_C)
print('log determinant fixed information:',logdet_info)
print('Restricted log-likelihood:',reml_ll)
assert np.isclose(reml_ll,reference['log_likelihood'],rtol=0,atol=1e-8)

title: Gaussian random slopes, penalized least squares and REML
text:
Fixed-effect uncertainty
At the fitted variance components, the plug-in covariance is
\[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta)=\hat\sigma^2(X^\top C^{-1}X)^{-1}.\]
The fixed triangular QR block supplies this through triangular solves. Standard errors are square roots of its diagonal. Our mixed-model z tests and 95% intervals are normal Wald approximations; this does not supply finite-group Student t degrees of freedom or variance-component confidence intervals.

R_inv=solve_triangular(qr_fixed,np.eye(x.shape[1]))
cov_beta=reml_variance*R_inv@R_inv.T
matrix_tex(cov_beta,r'\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta)')
print('Standard errors:',np.sqrt(cov_beta.diagonal()))
assert np.allclose(cov_beta,reference['covariance'],rtol=1e-8,atol=1e-8)

\(\displaystyle \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta)=\begin{bmatrix}46.575 & -1.4511 \\ -1.4511 & 2.3895\end{bmatrix}\)


Standard errors: [6.82455592 1.54578888]


The implementation is crates/stats-core/src/lmm.rs. Owned Vec inputs become nalgebra matrices; term/result structs preserve the array shapes and term order. Result propagates invalid designs, failed controls and nonconvergence to the PHP binding as exceptions. The binding validates and filters all aligned inputs, then returns plain arrays. No R process participates in application fitting.

title: Gaussian random slopes, penalized least squares and REML
section: Four grouping levels: which observations share variation?
text:
Four grouping levels: which observations share variation?
The same construction handles multiple nested terms. For repeated assessments within students, classes, schools and districts,
\[
y_i=x_i^\top\beta+d_{D(i)}+s_{S(i)}+c_{C(i)}+t_{T(i)}+\epsilon_i.
\]
Each term has its own Gaussian variance and is independent of the other terms. Conditional on the fixed design, two different observations share covariance only through common groups:
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(y_i,y_j\mid X)
=\tau_D^2\mathbf{1}_{D(i)=D(j)}
+\tau_S^2\mathbf{1}_{S(i)=S(j)}
+\tau_C^2\mathbf{1}_{C(i)=C(j)}
+\tau_T^2\mathbf{1}_{T(i)=T(j)},\quad i\ne j.
\]
On the diagonal, add the observation variance sigma² (or sigma²/w_i with weights). The grouping IDs must be globally unique within each term: a local school number needs its district in the key, and a local student number needs all its parents. Three grouping terms plus observations are often called a four-level model; here we name the number of grouping terms explicitly.

# Demonstrate the covariance implied by the fitted four-grouping-level model.
# This small matrix is for teaching; the native engine never constructs full V.
report=json.loads((ROOT/'docs/verifications/r-compatibility-results.json').read_text())
case=next(r for r in report['mixed'] if r['name']=='nested_4_grouping_levels_reml')
fit=case['PHP']['bobyqa']
input_case=next(r for r in fixtures['cases'] if r['name']==case['name'])
variances=np.array([t['covariance'][0][0] for t in fit['random']])
# First pair: same student; then different student, class, school and district.
selected=[0,1,4,8,16,32]
V=np.eye(len(selected))*fit['residual_variance']
for term,var in zip(input_case['terms'],variances):
    ids=np.array(term['groups'])[selected]
    V+=var*(ids[:,None]==ids[None,:])
display(pd.DataFrame(dict(grouping=['district','school','class','student'],
                          groups=[len(t['group_labels']) for t in fit['random']],
                          variance=variances)))
matrix_tex(V,r'V_{\mathrm{six\ observations}}')
print('Same student:',V[0,1])
print('Same class, different students:',V[0,2])
print('Same school, different classes:',V[0,3])
print('Same district, different schools:',V[0,4])
print('Different districts:',V[0,5])
assert np.isclose(V[0,1],variances.sum())
assert np.isclose(V[0,2],variances[:3].sum())
assert np.isclose(V[0,3],variances[:2].sum())
assert np.isclose(V[0,4],variances[0])
assert V[0,5]==0

title: Linear and generalized linear models
text: fit_lm() fits a linear model by least squares. fit_glm() fits a generalized linear model by maximum likelihood. Both take an R formula and named columns, as described in Model formulas.

title: Linear and generalized linear models
text:
Linear models
fit_lm() assumes independent errors with constant variance. Intervals and tests use Student’s t with df_residual degrees of freedom. The result has t_statistics, rss, residual_variance, sigma, r_squared and adj_r_squared. A first model shows a complete fit and its output.
fit_glm(family: 'gaussian') returns the same fit plus deviance, null_deviance and aic as R’s glm() reports them.

Each family’s matrix function in Matrix model functions defines these quantities exactly, including the null-deviance baseline and the convergence rule.

title: Linear and generalized linear models
text:
Weights and offsets
weights is an array aligned with the original rows, or the name of a numeric column. Weights must be positive, and a missing weight drops its row. For fit_lm() they are precision weights. For the binomial family they are integer trial counts, with the response given as proportions. Offsets are written in the formula with offset(expr). Several offsets are added together.

title: Linear and generalized linear models
text:
Differences from R

A rank-deficient design throws code 1004. R reports aliased coefficients as NA.
Zero weights are rejected. R gives such rows zero weight.
Gaussian fit_glm() intervals use t, as fit_lm() does. R’s confint.default() uses z and confint() profiles the likelihood.

Model formulas lists the remaining differences in formula handling.

title: Missing values and sample accounting
text: Every model function defaults to listwise deletion: a row with a missing value in any variable the model uses is left out of the fit. For the formula functions these are the variables the formula references, including weights, offsets and grouping factors; other columns may contain missing values. For the matrix functions they are the supplied predictors, outcome, weights, offsets and groups. The missing argument selects the policy:

title: Missing values and sample accounting
text:
What counts as missing
PHP null and floating-point NAN represent missing values. Positive and negative infinity are invalid numerical input, not missingness. Strings (including empty strings and ‘NA’), booleans, objects and absent/ragged matrix elements remain errors. Numeric zero is a valid value. No value is imputed or coerced from text.
Validation inspects all original values and shapes before deletion. A missing value cannot hide an invalid value or ragged row. After deletion, the retained fixed design must still have n > p (including the automatically added intercept) and full numerical rank. If no usable fit remains, the call throws. The Rust fit_ols() contract continues to require complete finite numeric vectors; the PHP binding implements the omission policy before calling it.

title: Missing values and sample accounting
text:
Warning and accounting
Every successful fit that omits observations emits one native PHP E_WARNING including the number dropped and original sample size. Complete data emits no warning. missing: ‘raise’ throws when missing values are found, without fitting. An unsuccessful fit throws rather than returning deletion metadata. Warning text is descriptive and is not a stable machine-readable interface.
Every successful result also includes:







Key
Meaning




n_input
int: original observations


n_observations
int: retained observations used in estimation


n_dropped
int: omitted observations


retained_rows
list: original zero-based iteration positions retained


dropped_rows
list: original zero-based iteration positions omitted



These positions refer to input iteration order, not PHP array keys. Each list is in ascending original order. fitted and residuals contain retained observations only, in retained_rows order; they are not padded with null. All statistics use the retained sample, including df_residual = n_observations - p. Metadata remains available even if warning display is disabled by PHP configuration.
foreach ($result['retained_rows'] as $outputPosition => $inputPosition) {
    $residualForOriginalPosition[$inputPosition] = $result['residuals'][$outputPosition];
}
Applications should use their normal warning handling to log or display the message and use the structured counts for reporting. PHP error handlers that promote warnings to exceptions can abort this call; use missing: ‘raise’ when omission should be prohibited explicitly. Warnings may be suppressed by PHP settings, so user-facing applications should also inspect n_dropped rather than rely only on display_errors. Do not suppress deletion without recording it.

title: Missing values and sample accounting
text:
Statistical interpretation and reference behavior
Listwise deletion is simple and preserves aligned observations, but changes the estimation sample. It does not guarantee unbiased results for arbitrary missingness. Report the excluded count and investigate why values are missing; this policy implements neither imputation nor a missing-data model.
R’s explicit na.action = na.omit and statsmodels’ explicit missing=‘drop’ provide comparable complete-case fits. Do not assume that every reference library warns on omission by default: warnings and metadata are our explicit contract. The three implementation verification checks identical retained samples and numerical results, with the PHP warning captured as evidence.
This changes the initial API, which rejected null and NAN. Existing callers that need that strict behavior should pass missing: ‘raise’. Other invalid inputs continue to be rejected. Helpers can still perform their own explicit preparation; when they omit data before the call, they must report it themselves because the extension can account only for rows it actually receives.

title: Missing values and sample accounting
text:
Logistic outcomes
fit_logistic() follows the same deletion, warning and row-accounting policy as fit_ols(). With default unit trial weights, numeric outcomes must be exactly 0 or 1, including rows with missing predictors. After deletion both classes must remain and n must exceed p; otherwise fitting fails. Its residuals are response residuals y - probability, and both residuals and fitted probabilities follow retained_rows order.

title: Missing values and sample accounting
text:
Probit and Poisson outcomes
Probit follows the binary rules above. Poisson validates nonnegative integer counts before deletion; after deletion at least one positive count must remain. All estimators warn once on a successful fit that dropped rows, expose original row positions, and support missing: ‘raise’. Zero Poisson counts are observed values, not missingness. Returned mean counts and residuals follow retained_rows.

title: Missing values and sample accounting
text:
Mixed-model group IDs
fit_mixed_intercept() deletes a row if x, y or the group ID is missing. Group missingness means null; NAN/float group IDs are invalid categorical labels and are rejected. Validation still covers every original value before deletion. Group labels and sizes describe the retained sample, and groups completely removed by deletion are absent from results. If deletion leaves only one group, all singletons or insufficient fixed-design observations, fitting fails. Inspect retained_rows to align conditional/population fits and both residual definitions with original data.

title: Missing values and sample accounting
text:
Expanded inputs
Optional weights/offsets and every random term’s z/groups participate in the same listwise deletion mask. Validate original lengths, types and values before deletion; preserve aligned rows across all vectors and terms. The fixed-model contracts now permit grouped-binomial proportions with positive integer trial weights. Invalid success/trial counts remain errors, even in rows that would otherwise be dropped. General mixed fits return one warning and original row positions just like the existing functions. These cases are tested in tests/r-compatibility.php and tests/lmm-expanded.php.
fit_logistic_mixed applies the same policy across x, proportions, groups, trial counts and offsets. Trial counts above 1,000,000 are rejected before deleting rows. Near-integer success encodings within tolerance are canonicalized only after original validation and deletion; zero-success/zero-failure samples then fail as required for a finite unpenalized fit.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
read_csv() reads a delimited text file into typed columns. It is the native reader behind phibble’s DataFrame::fromCsv(). Its records, names, guessed types, values, and problem messages match phibble’s PHP reader, which follows readr 2 (readr::read_delim()). phibble keeps name repair, col_select, factor and parse_number() columns, and the problems warning in PHP.
Phit\read_csv() is the narrower of the two readers. It has no select or name_repair option, its col_names takes a boolean rather than a list of names, and the readr letters f (factor) and n (number) have no type code here. DataFrame::fromCsv() supplies all of these in PHP around the native call.

The type codes are ? (guess), l (bool), i (int), d (double), c (string), D (date), T (datetime), and _ (skip). phibble reads f (factor) and n (number) columns by requesting c and parsing in PHP.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Result
[
    'names' => list<string>,
    'columns' => list<null|array{
        type: 'bool'|'int'|'float'|'string'|'date'|'datetime',
        values: list<bool|int|float|string|null>,
        failed: int,
    }>,
    'problems' => list<string>,
]
Values use phibble’s storage form. Bools, ints, and floats are PHP scalars and strings are strings. A date is an int count of days since 1970-01-01. A datetime is an int count of microseconds since the epoch in UTC. NA is null. A skipped column is null. failed counts values that did not parse under the column’s explicit or guessed type; those values are null. phibble turns nonzero counts into its column 'x': n values could not be parsed as type problems.
problems holds one entry per ragged row, such as row 7: expected 5 columns, got 4. The row number is the record’s position in the file, counting skipped lines and the header. A multi-line quoted field counts as one record. A file that ends inside a quoted field adds row N: unterminated quoted field at end of file.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Reading in chunks
Phit\CsvReader reads a file a chunk of rows at a time. It is the native reader behind phibble’s DataFrame::csvChunks() and fromCsvChunked(), which follow readr’s read_delim_chunked(). It holds the text of one chunk and one read block, so its memory follows the chunk size and not the file size.
$reader = new Phit\CsvReader(string $path, array $options = []);
$reader->names(): array;           // list<string>
$reader->next(int $rows): ?array;  // the next chunk, or null
The options are read_csv()’s. The constructor reads the header, so names() is available before the first chunk. It returns the header’s names, X1..Xn when col_names is false, or [] for an empty file. next() returns at most $rows rows in read_csv()’s result shape, with two more keys: position, the 1-based index of the chunk’s first row, and rows, the chunk’s row count. It returns null once no rows remain.
Chunks follow phibble’s chunked reader:

Types not given in types are guessed from the first chunk, from guess_max of its rows sampled as above. Every later chunk is parsed as those types. phibble sets guess_max to the chunk size by default, as readr does. A value in a later chunk that does not fit its column’s type counts in that chunk’s failed.
Problem rows are numbered from the start of the file. Each chunk carries the problems of its own rows.
The unterminated-quote problem goes with the last chunk. After each chunk the reader looks past blank lines to see whether records remain.
n_max caps the rows across all chunks.
A file with no data rows gives no chunks. The one exception is an unterminated quote in the header: next() then returns a chunk with no rows that carries the problem.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Records

Short rows are padded with NA. Long rows put the extra fields, joined by the delimiter, into the last column.
A UTF-8 byte order mark at the start of the file is removed before tokenizing (when skip is 0), so a quoted first header loses its quotes. One at the start of the first record after skipped lines is also removed.
LF and CRLF line endings are accepted. CR is read as the line ending when the first line break falls in a 4 MiB stretch of the file (counted from the first byte after skipped lines) that holds no LF. phibble reads 4 MiB blocks and decides from the first block with a line break, so the two agree. Otherwise a lone CR is data. Quoted fields can hold delimiters and line breaks, which are kept as written.
A line is blank when its raw text holds nothing but spaces, tabs and carriage returns. That is the raw line and not the parsed fields, so a quoted empty string is a field holding data, and it does not depend on trim_ws or on the delimiter: a line of spaces is blank even when the delimiter is a space. Under skip_empty_rows a blank line is dropped; otherwise it is tokenized like any other line, so an empty line is one empty field and a wider data frame records it as one column short. A last line the file left unterminated is never dropped, so a\n is two rows and a\n \n is one.
An unterminated quote at the end of the file closes the field there.
Bytes are passed through unchanged. There is no encoding validation.
An empty file, or one with only empty lines, returns no names and no columns. When the header is read and no data rows are, the names come back with empty columns typed string, following readr, which reads a header-only file as text. Four cases reach that state: n_max: 0, a header-only file, a skip that leaves no row after the header, and every row empty under skip_empty_rows. An explicit code in types still applies.

phibble tokenizes by vroom’s (readr 2’s) quote rules with a fast reader when it can (no comment, "" escapes, no backslash escapes, and a quote character) and with its own character-level reader otherwise. The native reader reproduces both. The two differ in small ways:

In the fast reader, a field is quoted when its first byte is the quote. Inside it, every lone quote toggles quoting and is dropped, and a doubled quote is a literal quote, so "x "y" z" reads as x y z. Quotes in an unquoted field are literal.
The character-level reader folds CRLF to LF everywhere, including inside quotes. A quote opens a quoted section only when the field so far is whitespace. Text after the comment prefix ends the record, so a line holding only spaces and a comment is a one-field record holding those spaces, unless no record has been read yet: before the first one, a comment prefix with only whitespace in front of it drops the line, as readr drops it.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Guessing
Values are trimmed and NA-mapped first. The guess uses every row when there are at most guess_max. Otherwise it uses guess_max - 1 evenly spaced rows (step = intdiv(rows, guess_max): rows 0, step, 2·step, and so on) plus the last row, as vroom does. The first rule that fits every sampled value wins.

bool: T F TRUE FALSE True False true false t f.
int: an optional sign, then digits with optional grouping marks between them, that fits in 64 bits. An unsigned leading zero (007) stays text; 0 and -07 are ints.
double: [+-]inf or [+-]nan (any case), or a decimal number with an optional decimal mark, exponent, and grouping marks. 1. and 1, qualify. The leading-zero rule applies: 0e5 and 00.5 stay text.
date: YYYY-MM-DD or YYYY/MM/DD (the separators may differ).
datetime: YYYY-MM-DD[(T| )HH[:MM[:SS[.fraction]]]][Z|±HH[[:]MM]].
Otherwise string.

An all-NA column with at least one data row is bool. phibble differs from readr in one rule: whole numbers guess as int, where readr guesses double. The date and datetime rules check only the shape. A column whose values look like dates guesses date even when a value is not a calendar date, and that value then fails to parse.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Parsing
The column’s type is applied to every row. A guessed numeric column allows the grouping mark. An explicitly typed one does not, as in phibble.

bool also accepts 1 and 0.
int accepts leading zeros and a + sign.
double accepts PHP numeric strings (when the decimal mark is .), inf and nan, and the guessing grammar.
date needs a valid calendar date in years 0001 to 9999.
datetime needs a valid date, hours up to 23, and minutes and seconds up to 59. Fractions are truncated to microseconds. An offset converts to UTC and no offset means UTC. Offsets up to ±24:59 are accepted, as by PHP’s DateTimeImmutable. A date alone is midnight UTC.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Errors
A missing or unreadable file and invalid options throw \ValueError (not the statistical exception). Invalid options include an unknown key, a wrong value type, a multi-byte delimiter, quote, decimal mark, or grouping mark, an unknown type code, and a negative skip or n_max. The decimal and grouping marks must differ and cannot be a digit, sign, e, E, or newline.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Differences from readr
These follow phibble’s reader:

Whole numbers guess as int.
With a comment prefix, a value followed by a comment is trimmed (2 # x reads as 2).
Date and datetime guessing checks the shape only.
In a file whose only line ending is CR, readr skips a blank line only before the first record and keeps the interior and trailing ones; both readers read CR as the line ending and then apply the blank-line rule throughout.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Performance
On an Apple Silicon Mac with PHP 8.5, a 1,000,000-row file with int, float, string, date, and datetime columns (59 MB) reads in about 0.11 seconds, including building the PHP arrays. phibble’s csv_guess benchmark (1,000,000 rows) takes 0.12 seconds through DataFrame::fromCsv() with the extension and 1.0 seconds with phibble’s PHP reader.

title: Reading CSV files
text:
Verification
tests/csv.php checks quoting, escapes, NA handling, trimming, every option, every type code, the guessing rules, datetimes, ragged rows, chunks, and the error cases.
tests/csv-conformance.php checks read_csv() against phibble’s reader without a phibble checkout. phibble generates tests/fixtures/csv-conformance.json from its own PHP reader with bin/generate-csv-conformance, and this repository commits a byte-identical copy. The file holds 108 cases: every option at its default and at one other value, all eight type codes, ragged rows, a BOM, CRLF and CR line endings, an unterminated quote, comments, an empty file, bytes that are not valid UTF-8, the four ways to read no data rows, and the blank-line rule in its eighteen shapes. Each case records the input, the options, and the names, types, values, failure counts, and problems phibble produces. The suite requires read_csv() to reproduce all of it, so a change in either reader fails in its own repository. It reads every case again at block sizes of 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, and 64 bytes, and through CsvReader in one chunk and in chunks of 1, 2, and 3 rows. One chunk must equal the whole read. Small chunks must give the same problems in order and, read as text, the same values.
The copy is pinned. tests/fixtures/PHIBBLE_REFERENCE names the phibble commit it came from, and bin/fetch-csv-fixtures copies the file from that commit, either from a local checkout given as its first argument or in PHIBBLE_REPO, or from a clone of the repository named in the pin. Refreshing the corpus means regenerating it in phibble, moving the pin, and running that script.
phibble’s reader does not report an unterminated quoted field and read_csv() does. Each case therefore carries a closed list of the extra problems read_csv() is expected to add, and the suite compares its problems with the union rather than filtering by pattern, so an unexpected problem fails.
tests/csv-phibble.php is the deep tier and runs when PHIBBLE_AUTOLOAD points at phibble’s vendor/autoload.php. It compares both readers through DataFrame::fromCsv() on the fixtures and on thousands of random files and option combinations, with the case count and the seed taken from CSV_FUZZ_CASES and CSV_FUZZ_SEED. It requires identical names, types, values, and warnings. With a phibble that has DataFrame::csvChunks(), it also compares CsvReader with phibble’s PHP chunked reader on random files, chunk sizes, and native block sizes (CSV_CHUNK_CASES of them). It requires the same chunks, positions, types, values, and per-chunk warnings, in the same order.

title: phit
text:
phit is a PHP extension, written in Rust, for statistical models. It fits linear, logistic, probit, Poisson and mixed-effects regression models, and evaluates probability distributions and descriptive statistics. Data go in as ordinary PHP arrays and results come back as associative arrays, with no model objects or services.
Models are written as R formulas: rent ~ area + district models rent from floor area and district. Factors, interactions and transformations such as log(area) are written in the formula, and phit builds the numeric design from named columns.
A first model runs this example with its data and explains each part of the result.

title: phit
text:
What phit provides

Regression models: fit_lm() and fit_glm() for linear, logistic, probit and Poisson regression, with weights and offsets. See Linear and generalized linear models.
Mixed models: fit_lmer() for Gaussian models with random intercepts and slopes, and fit_glmer() for a binomial model with a random intercept. See Mixed models.
Prediction on new data with confidence and prediction intervals.
Probability distributions: densities, CDFs, survival functions and quantiles for 12 families (13 parameterizations), and seeded random samples, including uniform, categorical and permutation sampling. See Probability distributions and Seeded sampling.
Descriptive statistics: means, variances, quantiles, weighted statistics, kernel density estimates and the ECDF. See Descriptive statistics.
Posterior draws: weighted moments and transforms for MCMC output. See Posterior draws.
CSV input: a native reader used by phibble. See Reading CSV files.

Each model also has a function over numeric matrices, such as fit_ols() and fit_logistic(), for code that builds its own design matrix. See Matrix model functions.

title: phit
text:
Results
Results follow R’s conventions: coefficient names, treatment contrasts, the order of terms, deviance and AIC as glm() reports them, and lme4’s REML estimates. Rows with missing values are dropped with a warning, and every result reports which rows it used. Errors are PHP exceptions with stable numeric codes. The verification pages compare each model with R, lme4 and statsmodels, and record the tolerances.

title: phit
text:
Requirements
phit runs on PHP 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5 (non-thread-safe builds) on Linux and macOS. It installs with PIE, or from prebuilt Linux binaries. See Installation. The pure-PHP polyfill provides the same functions where the extension cannot be installed, at lower speed.

title: Model formulas
text:
The formula functions accept an R model formula and a data set of named columns. They build R’s model matrix in Rust and call the same estimation cores as the matrix functions. Results keep each matrix function’s complete contract and add coefficient names.
PHP reflection reports $data and $weights as mixed. The generated stubs document the accepted types.

title: Model formulas
Model formulas
text:
Data
$data is an associative array of columns, name => list of values. An object is also accepted. The extension calls its public toModelData() method, or toColumns() when the first method is absent, and uses the returned array. Exceptions thrown by those methods propagate unchanged. phibble’s DataFrame::toModelData() returns this shape.
Each column is one of the following.

Numbers: integers and floats. null and NAN are missing. Infinity raises 1003.
Booleans: a logical column. R codes it as a two-level factor named {col}TRUE.
Strings: a character column. It becomes a factor whose levels are the distinct retained values in byte (C-locale) order, which is R’s order under LC_COLLATE=C. Other R locales can sort mixed-case or accented strings differently.
A factor descriptor: an array with exactly the keys levels (list of unique strings), codes (list of 0-based integers, null for missing), and ordered (bool). Levels keep the caller’s order and the first level is the reference.
Dates arrive as numbers, for example days or seconds since the epoch.

Every column must have the same length (code 1002). Only the columns a formula uses are type-checked. An unknown column, a malformed factor descriptor, or a referenced list-column or mixed-type column raises 1001. A list of row arrays raises 1001.

title: Model formulas
text:
Formula syntax
The formula grammar and operator precedence follow R.







Syntax
Meaning




y ~ a + b
Main effects. ~ a + b (no response) is valid for model_matrix.


- 1, + 0, 0 +
Remove the intercept. + 1 restores it.


a:b
Interaction columns for every combination of the coded variables.


a * b
a + b + a:b.


(a + b + c)^2
All main effects and interactions up to order 2.


a / b
a + a:b (nesting). b %in% a is b:a.


- term
Remove a term, for example a * b - a:b.


.
Every data column that does not appear in the response.


offset(expr)
A fixed known offset. Several offsets are summed.


(x | g), (x || g)
Random-effect terms (see below).



Terms are ordered as R orders them: main effects first, then two-way interactions, and so on, with ties in formula order. Within an interaction, variables appear in order of first appearance in the formula, and the first variable varies fastest in the column order. y ~ b:a + a therefore gives bv:ap, bv:aq, and so on.

Inline transforms
The following functions can appear as variables or inside one another. Column names are R’s deparsed expressions, including R’s spacing and its 15-digit number formatting, for example I(x^2), I(area/beds), I(x * 1e+05), and log(x, base = 2).

log(x), log(x, base), log2, log10, log1p, exp, expm1, sqrt, abs, sin, cos, and tan.
I(expr) with + - * / ^, numbers, parentheses, unary minus, comparisons (< > <= >= == !=), &, |, and !. A comparison gives a logical column, such as I(x > 3)TRUE. Strings compare with character and factor columns: I(region == "north").
poly(x, degree) gives R’s orthogonal polynomials and poly(x, degree, raw = TRUE) gives raw powers. Columns are named poly(x, 2)1, poly(x, 2)2, and so on. Orthogonal polynomials are computed over all input rows before deletion, as in R, and reject missing values. Raw polynomials allow them.
factor(x), as.factor(x), and ordered(x) convert a column. Numeric levels are sorted numerically and labelled with R’s number formatting. Levels come from all input rows, as in R’s model frame.
as.numeric(f) gives 1-based factor codes.
cbind(successes, failures) is a binomial response for fit_glm and fit_glmer.

Any other function raises 1007. A transform result of NaN, such as log(-1), is missing and is deleted like any other missing value (R also removes it, with a “NaNs produced” warning). An infinite result, such as log(0), raises 1003.


Contrasts
Unordered factors, strings, and logicals use treatment contrasts. The columns are named {variable}{level} for every level after the first. Ordered factors use contr.poly, with columns .L, .Q, .C, ^4, and so on. R’s coding rule decides whether a factor in a term receives contrasts or one indicator per level. A factor is coded by contrasts when the term without it appears earlier in the formula, or is empty. Without an intercept, the first factor in the first term that contains one receives full indicator coding. These rules give R’s columns for formulas such as y ~ 0 + f, y ~ x:f, y ~ f:g, and y ~ f * g - 1.

title: Model formulas
text:
Missing values and unused levels
Listwise deletion uses only the variables that the formula references. These include the response, transforms, offsets, weights, grouping factors, and random-effect columns. Other columns may contain missing values. As in the matrix functions, missing: 'drop' removes incomplete rows with one E_WARNING, and missing: 'raise' raises 1001. retained_rows and dropped_rows are original zero-based positions.
model_matrix keeps unused factor levels, as R’s model.matrix() does, and their indicator columns are all zero. The fitting functions drop levels that are absent after deletion, as lm(), glm(), lmer(), and glmer() do through drop.unused.levels = TRUE. Character levels always come from the retained rows.

title: Model formulas
text:
model_matrix
The result has these keys.







Key
Contents




y
Response values. A factor response gives 0-based codes plus response_levels. cbind(s, f) gives [s, f] rows. null without a response.


x
Design rows for retained observations, including (Intercept) when present.


columns, assign
R column names and R’s assign attribute (0 for the intercept).


terms, intercept
R term labels and whether the intercept is present.


formula, response
The deparsed formula and response expression.


offset
Summed offsets, or null.


random
One entry per random-effect term: label, group, columns, correlated, z, groups.


n_input, n_observations, n_dropped, retained_rows, dropped_rows
Deletion accounting.



x includes the intercept column. Pass it to a matrix function with intercept: false. Each random entry has the shape that fit_mixed expects:
$mm = Phit\model_matrix('y ~ x + (1 + x | g)', $data);
$fit = Phit\fit_mixed(x: $mm['x'], y: $mm['y'], random: $mm['random'], intercept: false);

title: Model formulas
text:
fit_lm and fit_glm
fit_lm calls the fit_ols core and returns its full result. fit_glm supports four family and link combinations. An empty link selects the canonical link.








Family
Links
Core




gaussian
identity
fit_ols, plus deviance, null_deviance, and aic as R’s glm() reports them


binomial
logit, probit
fit_logistic, fit_probit


poisson
log
fit_poisson



Other families or links raise 1007. A binomial response can be 0/1 numbers, booleans, a factor or character column (the first level is failure and all other levels are success, as in R), proportions with integer trial weights, or cbind(successes, failures).
$weights is either an array aligned with the original rows or the name of a numeric column. Missing weights delete their rows. Weights must be positive.
Formula fits add these keys to the matrix result: formula, response, columns (aligned with coefficients), terms, assign, intercept, and named (column => coefficient), and predvars. predvars holds the state that prediction must reuse: each factor’s levels after deletion and each orthogonal poly() basis’s recurrence coefficients (R’s xlevels and predvars). fit_glm also returns family and link. All list keys of the matrix functions are unchanged.
Random-effect terms in fit_lm or fit_glm raise 1007 and name fit_lmer and fit_mixed as the alternatives.

title: Model formulas
text:
fit_lmer and fit_glmer
fit_lmer maps lme4-style bars onto fit_mixed. REML is the default, as in lme4::lmer(). Supported bars include (1 | g), (x | g), (0 + x | g), (x || g) (diagonal covariance), several terms such as (1 | g1) + (1 | g2), interaction groups (1 | g1:g2), and nesting (1 | g1/g2). Nesting expands to (1 | g1) + (1 | g2:g1), with lme4’s group name and g2level:g1level labels. The result is the fit_mixed contract. Each random entry also has label, group, columns, and correlated. Its effects_cond_var lists one k×k conditional covariance per group, in group_labels order. These are the blocks that ranef(fit, condVar = TRUE) attaches as postVar. For (x || g), lme4 reports only the diagonal of each block.
fit_glmer supports exactly one random intercept (1 | g) with the binomial family and logit link, over the fit_logistic_mixed core. quadraturePoints corresponds to lme4’s nAGQ. Responses follow fit_glm. random_effects_cond_var gives the conditional variance of each group’s mode, as lme4’s postVar.

title: Model formulas
text:
Prediction: predict
predict($fit, $newdata) predicts from any formula fit, as R’s predict() does for lm, glm and merMod objects. It rebuilds the fit’s formula over $newdata, which needs the predictor columns but not the response.
$fit = Phit\fit_glm('am ~ wt + poly(hp, 2)', $cars, family: 'binomial');
$p = Phit\predict($fit, ['wt' => [2.2, 3.4], 'hp' => [95, 180]], type: 'response', seFit: true);
// $p['fit'] probabilities, $p['se_fit'] delta-method standard errors

Factors are coded with the levels the fit saw. A level the fit never saw raises 1001 with R’s message (factor g has new level z). Logical and character columns work the same way.
poly(x, k) evaluates the fitted orthogonal basis at the new values, as R’s predict.poly() does. It is not refitted to the new data.
offset() terms are evaluated over $newdata and added.
A row with a missing predictor predicts null and is listed in missing_rows. Every list has one entry per $newdata row.
type: 'link' (the default) returns the linear predictor. type: 'response' applies the inverse link, and seFit then uses the delta method, as R does.
interval: 'confidence' or 'prediction' adds lower and upper for fit_lm fits, using t with df_residual at level. A prediction interval adds the residual variance; as in R, it assumes constant variance for a weighted fit.
For fit_lmer and fit_glmer fits, predictions add each known group’s random effects (lme4’s default re.form = NULL). random: false gives population predictions (re.form = NA), and the grouping columns can then be absent. An unseen group raises 1001 unless allowNewLevels: true, which predicts it at the population level. Mixed predictions have no standard errors, as in lme4.

GLM standard errors use the covariance at the final coefficients. R’s predict.glm() uses vcov(), which reuses the last IRLS weights (see R compatibility). The two agree to about 1e-5 relative on well-conditioned fits and can differ by about 1e-4 near separation.

title: Model formulas
text:
Differences from R

Character levels use byte order. R’s default locale collation can order mixed-case or non-ASCII strings differently.
Rank-deficient designs raise 1004. R reports NA (aliased) coefficients instead.
Weights must be positive. R accepts zero weights. cbind() rows with zero trials are rejected; R gives them zero weight.
A response that also appears on the right-hand side raises 1001. R drops the term with a warning.
Only the functions listed above can be evaluated. factor() takes one argument, and poly() takes one variable.
x %in% a is labelled x:a. R labels the term x %in% a; the columns are identical.
model_matrix returns factor responses as 0-based codes with response_levels.
fit_glm(family: 'gaussian') uses t-based intervals, as fit_ols does. R’s confint.default() is z-based and confint() profiles the likelihood.
fit_lmer orders groups and effects by first appearance after deletion and keeps random terms in formula order. lme4 sorts levels and orders terms by their number of levels. Estimates are invariant to these orderings.
Duplicate column names collapse in the named map; columns keeps every name.

title: Model formulas
text:
Verification
tests/generate-formula-fixtures.R saves 62 R references under LC_COLLATE=C: 33 model.frame()/model.matrix() designs, 14 lm() fits, and 15 glm() fits. They use the repository’s housing, schools, learning, clinic, and cbpp data and a seeded synthetic data frame with factors, unused and reordered levels, ordered factors, logicals, character columns, missing values, weights, offsets, transforms, and no-intercept models. glm() references are restarted from R’s own solution until the coefficients stop changing, because the default deviance criterion fixes coefficients only to about the square root of its tolerance. tests/formula.php compares design columns, terms, and rows exactly, design values within 1e-12 relative, and fit quantities within the matrix suites’ 1e-9 + 1e-7*abs(reference).
tests/generate-formula-lme4-fixtures.R saves 10 lme4 references (7 lmer() and 3 glmer() fits), including crossed, nested, correlated, and uncorrelated terms and adaptive quadrature. The references include the ranef(condVar = TRUE) conditional variances, which are also compared for fit_mixed_intercept on the ML schools case. tests/formula-mixed.php uses the tolerances of the existing lme4 suites.
tests/generate-predict-fixtures.R saves 25 predict() references: lm() with orthogonal poly(), factors, logicals, ordered interactions, offsets, weights, no intercept, standard errors, and confidence and prediction intervals; glm() on the link and response scales for every family and link (including cbind() responses and offsets); and lmer()/glmer() conditional, population and response-scale predictions with an unseen group. The new data include values outside the fitted range, missing rows and a factor whose level set differs from the fit. GLM standard errors are compared tightly with the final-coefficient value recomputed in R and loosely (1e-3 relative) with R’s own se.fit. tests/predict.php also checks that predicting the training data reproduces the fitted values, and the error messages. All fixtures are indexed in the reference manifest.

title: Posterior-draw numerical kernels
text: These kernels support a separate PHP CmdStan interface’s PSIS-LOO moment matching. They compute weighted moments, covariance maps and affine transformations using nalgebra in stats-core. The PHP extension supplies strict numeric conversion and ordinary array results. The caller owns Stan model evaluation, importance ratios, PSIS, iteration control and diagnostics. These functions also work on other literal numeric matrices. They add no fitting, plotting or model abstraction.

title: Posterior-draw numerical kernels
text:
Weighted moments
For \(X\in\mathbb R^{S\times P}\), normalize nonnegative weights to \(w_i\) with \(\sum_i w_i=1\). A null weights argument selects \(w_i=1/S\).
\[
\mu=\sum_i w_i x_i,\qquad
C_{\mathrm{pop}}=\sum_i w_i(x_i-\mu)(x_i-\mu)^T,\qquad
C_{\mathrm{unbiased}}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{pop}}}{1-\sum_i w_i^2}.
\]
Unbiased normalization uses reliability weights, not frequency/replication counts. Multiplying all supplied weights by a positive constant does not change the result. Uniform weights give divisor \(S\) for population covariance and \(S-1\) for unbiased covariance. A singular covariance is a legitimate moment result.
Weights are divided by their maximum before compensated summation and normalization, so a finite weight array whose ordinary sum would overflow still works. Means use an anchor from a positive-weight draw, a compensated sum of deviations, and a second correction pass. Covariance uses compensated centered cross-products and is returned exactly symmetric. This avoids cancellation from a large common offset. Zero-weight rows contribute nothing but still undergo full validation. The unbiased denominator is evaluated as \(1-\sum_i w_i^2\) in binary64; a zero or negative computed denominator is explicitly rejected, including concentrations that round to one effective draw. No extra effective-sample-size cutoff is imposed.

title: Posterior-draw numerical kernels
text:
Covariance map and tolerances
Use lower Cholesky factors \(C_s=L_sL_s^T\), \(C_t=L_tL_t^T\) and solve
\[
L_s^T A^T=L_t^T,\qquad A C_s A^T=C_t.
\]
No matrix inverse is formed. The returned log Jacobian is \(\sum_j\log (L_{t,jj})-\log(L_{s,jj})\), so a very large or small determinant need not be representable as a floating-point number. The map depends on parameter order and is one of many possible covariance maps.
Let \(d_i=\sqrt{C_{ii}}\) and \(R_{ij}=C_{ij}/d_i/d_j\). Each diagonal must be strictly positive. Before Cholesky, compare opposite standardized entries \(a,b\):
\[
|a-b|\le64\epsilon\max(1,|a|,|b|),\qquad \epsilon=2^{-52}.
\]
Accepted rounding-level asymmetry is averaged on this standardized scale. The Cholesky factor of \(R\) must exist, and each squared diagonal pivot must exceed \(64\epsilon P\). Then rescale its rows by \(d_i\) to recover the original covariance’s factor. These relative checks are invariant to changing individual parameter units within representable arithmetic. They define a pivot-based numerical-singularity policy, not a guarantee of a particular condition number. Near the threshold, rounding and parameter order can affect acceptance. No diagonal jitter, ridge, eigenvalue clipping or fallback factorization is performed. Singular moment covariance may therefore be returned by draws_moments and explicitly rejected by draws_covariance_map.

title: Posterior-draw numerical kernels
text:
Affine transformation and determinant
For each draw interpreted as a column vector, \(y_i=A x_i+b\). Because PHP draw matrices have draws in rows, the implementation uses \(Y=X A^T+\mathbf1 b^T\). There is no intercept column or change of draw order.
To assess invertibility, divide each row of \(A\) by its largest absolute element, then divide each column of that scaled matrix by its largest absolute element. Zero rows/columns are singular. On the equilibrated matrix \(B\), require
\[
\sigma_{\min}(B)>64\epsilon P\sigma_{\max}(B).
\]
SVD assesses numerical rank; pivoted LU supplies log absolute diagonal pivots. The returned log determinant adds the logs of all row and column scales. Summing logs avoids determinant overflow/underflow, and absolute pivots support reflections and negative determinants. The code forms no inverse. Division rather than a reciprocal handles subnormal scales. Numerical singularity raises 1004.
All arithmetic uses binary64. Finite inputs may still cause nonfinite intermediate or final arithmetic at extreme scales; this raises 1003 rather than returning NAN/INF. These kernels do not guarantee relative accuracy for underflow-sized covariances or arbitrarily ill-conditioned inputs.

title: Posterior-draw numerical kernels
Posterior-draw numerical kernels
text:
Independent verification
tests/generate-draw-fixtures.py produces 25 cases using only Python’s standard library Decimal at 80-digit precision. It implements weighted formulas with scalar loops, a scalar Cholesky and backward solve, and independent pivoted Gauss-Jordan for reference inverse/log determinants. It never calls the extension or nalgebra. The saved tests/fixtures/draws-python.json records the Python version, algorithm and tolerances. The provenance manifest hashes the generator and fixture, input options and compared quantities. R/Python are unnecessary for ordinary tests.
Rust and PHP compare all fixture outputs at \(10^{-11}+10^{-11}|\mathrm{reference}|\). Extreme-scale nonzero affine outputs and covariance identities also use \(10^{-12}\) relative error. Affine round trips and summed forward/reverse log determinants use the ordinary absolute-plus-relative tolerance. Tests cover correlated parameters, uniform/nonuniform/zero weights, weight rescaling, one effective draw, singular covariance, one parameter, large offsets, mixed units, nontrivial orientation, reflections, determinant overflow/underflow, invalid arrays and threshold behavior. Rust also checks weighted covariance transformation under both normalizations. PHP verifies named arguments, defaults, array iteration order and strict rejection without missing-row warnings. Existing regression tests preserve their contracts.
python3 tests/generate-draw-fixtures.py # Intentional reference refresh
python3 scripts/reference-manifest.py
cargo test -p stats-core --locked --test draws
php -n -d "extension=$STATS_EXTENSION" tests/draws.php
PHP=/path/to/matching/php PHP_CONFIG=/path/to/php-config ./scripts/check
Reproducible API-level benchmarks compare full outputs to R before measuring moments, maps and affine transformations on representative sizes.

title: Probability distributions
text: The extension provides 182 probability-evaluation functions: 13 parameterizations, seven operations each, and scalar plus native _array forms, plus 13 explicitly seeded batch sampling functions. Uniform, categorical and permutation samplers have no probability functions and are described there. These return ordinary PHP numbers and arrays. Distribution evaluation is separate from regression fitting; fit_poisson() still fits a count model, while dist_poisson_pmf() evaluates a specified Poisson distribution. Descriptive statistics add ten functions for supplied numeric slices. Posterior-draw kernels handle literal draw matrices.

title: Probability distributions
text:
Families and parameterizations
Replace {family} in the operation names below with one of these names. PHP numeric arguments accept integers or floats; binomial size specifically requires an integer. All parameters must be finite and satisfy their domains.








Family
Parameters in call order
Support and conventions




normal
mean = 0, sd = 1
Real line; sd > 0


t
df
Standard Student t; df > 0, no location/scale arguments


chisquare
df
Nonnegative; df > 0


f
df1, df2
Nonnegative; numerator/denominator df both positive


beta
alpha, beta
[0,1]; both shape parameters positive


gamma
shape, scale = 1
Nonnegative; both positive; mean shape * scale


exponential
rate = 1
Nonnegative; positive rate; mean 1/rate


lognormal
meanlog = 0, sdlog = 1
Positive; log X is Normal(meanlog, sdlog); sdlog > 0


logistic
location = 0, scale = 1
Real line; positive scale


binomial
size, prob
Integer successes 0..size; size 0..2^53, prob [0,1]


poisson
lambda
Nonnegative integer counts; lambda nonnegative


nbinom
size, prob
Failures before size-th success; real size > 0, prob (0,1]


nbinom_mu
size, mu
Same negative binomial; size > 0, mu ≥ 0; variance mu + mu^2/size



Gamma’s second parameter is scale, exponential’s is rate. Negative-binomial size is a positive real dispersion/shape parameter, not a binomial trial count. The two NB forms are equivalent when prob = size/(size + mu). Poisson lambda zero, binomial size zero/prob zero/prob one, and NB prob one/mu zero represent point masses. Parameter conversion in the mean-form NB avoids overflowing size + mu.

title: Probability distributions
text:
Scalar and batch operations








Operation
Scalar function
Definition




Density
dist_{family}_pdf(x, ...parameters)
Continuous density f(x)


Log density
dist_{family}_logpdf(x, ...parameters)
Natural log of density


Mass
dist_{family}_pmf(k, ...parameters)
Discrete P(X = k)


Log mass
dist_{family}_logpmf(k, ...parameters)
Natural log of mass


CDF
dist_{family}_cdf(x_or_k, ...parameters)
P(X ≤ x)


Log CDF
dist_{family}_logcdf(x_or_k, ...parameters)
ln P(X ≤ x)


Survival
